questions.stem: _______ is the process of selecting appropriate query execution strategy?
questions.hint: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 5

answer.text: Query optimization
answer.explanation: Selecting an efficient execution strategy is optimization. A tree or graph represents the query; processing is the broader transformation and execution activity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A graph corresponds to relational calculus, not strategy selection. (PDF pp. 27, 34.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The module explicitly defines optimization as choosing an efficient strategy. (PDF pp. 27, 34.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A query tree represents relational algebra and operations. (PDF pp. 27, 34.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Processing includes decomposition and execution as well as optimization. (PDF pp. 27, 34.)

evidence.quote: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.
Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.
A query graph represents the predicate relationships of a relational-calculus expression without itself prescribing an operator execution order.

questions.stem: Which update-timing policy permits a transaction's changes to reach the persistent database before the transaction commits?
questions.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 22

answer.text: Immediate update
answer.explanation: Immediate update permits a transaction's changes to be written to the persistent database before commit. If that transaction later aborts, recovery may need to undo those changes. Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database. In-place update describes overwriting an existing location, while shadow update describes writing a separate version. Those location strategies do not, by their names alone, specify the timing policy requested here. Immediate update need not flush every cache write immediately.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Describes overwriting the existing location, not the commit-timing policy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct: immediate update permits persistent database changes before commit and may require undo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Describes writing a separate version while preserving the committed one, not the requested timing policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deferred update excludes uncommitted changes from the persistent database.

evidence.quote: Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.
In-place update overwrites the original location.

questions.stem: Which query-optimization approach applies relational-algebra properties and equivalences to rewrite a query and reduce intermediate work?
questions.hint: Consider which equivalent transformation changes intermediate work and what assumptions preserve meaning.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 26

answer.text: Heuristic approach
answer.explanation: Heuristic optimization uses algebraic rules to reduce intermediate work, for example applying selective filters earlier, replacing a product plus join predicate with a join and projecting away unneeded columns. Storage and execution without rewriting do not perform those transformations. Cost estimation predicts resources for candidate plans rather than naming the algebraic rewrite approach itself. A practical optimizer can combine rewriting and costing, but the question isolates the rule-based transformation role.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect: storage without rewriting does not transform the algebraic query representation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct: heuristic rewriting uses operator properties and equivalences to reduce intermediate work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incorrect: repeatable execution without rewriting does not apply the requested query transformations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: cost estimation predicts candidate-plan resource use rather than identifying the algebraic rewrite approach.

evidence.quote: Heuristics reduce intermediate work: push selective row filters toward base tables; replace product followed by a join predicate with a join; project unneeded columns away while retaining join/filter columns; reorder inner joins when equivalence permits; reuse common expressions when worthwhile. Split conjunctive selections when each predicate can be applied earlier to its own input.
A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic.

questions.stem: In which phase of the two phase locking protocol can a transaction obtain locks?
questions.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 46
Computer Science Exit Exam practice questions · Question 38

answer.text: Growing phase
answer.explanation: Two-phase locking acquires locks in the growing phase, then releases them in the shrinking phase without acquiring new ones.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Release is the unlocking portion, not acquisition. (PDF pp. 86.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rollback is not one of the two acquisition/release phases. (PDF pp. 86.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shrinking forbids new locks. (PDF pp. 86.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Growing allows acquisition and forbids release. (PDF pp. 86.)

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is not problem if concurrency is not controlled properly?
questions.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 53

answer.text: Consistent database
answer.explanation: Lost update, temporary update/dirty read, and incorrect summary are concurrency problems. A consistent database is the desired outcome of concurrency control.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Lost update is explicitly a concurrency anomaly. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistency is a desired state, so this is the exception. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incorrect summary mixes values from different update stages. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Dirty read exposes an update before its transaction has safely committed. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

evidence.quote: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.
Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.
A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work.

questions.stem: During restart recovery after a crash, which operation removes the database effects of a transaction that had not committed?
questions.hint: Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 79

answer.text: Rollback
answer.explanation: Atomicity requires removing the effects of an incomplete transaction after a crash. Rollback performs that undo work, restoring before-images as needed. Commit instead accepts successful transaction effects, and a view is a query representation rather than a recovery action. Redo installs logged after-images to recover missing work; it does not name the removal of uncommitted effects requested here. These actions occur during restart recovery after the system is operating again.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect: a view is not an operation that reverses transaction effects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Incorrect: commit accepts transaction effects rather than undoing the incomplete work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Correct: rollback undoes the effects of the uncommitted transaction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: redo installs logged after-images; the requested removal requires undo/rollback.

evidence.quote: Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects. Rollback handles failed/uncommitted work; redo preserves committed work missing from pages; checkpoints reduce log-search work; backups provide another stored copy.
Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.
A view is a stored query definition, not encryption.

questions.stem: A system is in a ______ state if there exists a set of transactions such that every transaction in the set is waiting for another transaction in the set.
questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 81

answer.text: Deadlock
answer.explanation: Mutual waiting among transactions for locks held by one another is a deadlock condition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Idle does not express mutual lock waiting. (PDF pp. 87.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Waiting alone need not involve a cycle. (PDF pp. 87.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deadlock is mutual waiting that prevents progress. (PDF pp. 87.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ready does not describe transactions blocked on one another. (PDF pp. 87.)

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.
A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.

questions.stem: Users may request permitted aggregates but must not infer protected individual values by subtracting overlapping aggregate answers. Which security measure specifically addresses this indirect-disclosure threat?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario concerns identity, permission, disclosure or valid values.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 15

answer.text: A. Inference control
answer.explanation: Inference control targets learning protected individual facts from aggregate answers. For example, subtracting a sum excluding one person from a sum including that person can reveal their value even when their row is hidden. Ordinary access control grants or denies actions, integrity validates data and encryption protects encoded content. The specified indirect-disclosure threat identifies inference control specifically.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This directly prevents disclosure of individual facts inferred from allowed aggregates.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Authorization alone does not prevent inference from otherwise allowed answers.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Integrity constrains valid data rather than indirect disclosure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encryption does not stop an authorized user combining decrypted aggregate answers.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Inference control directly matches the threat.

evidence.quote: Authentication establishes identity; authorization/access control determines permitted actions. Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions. A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges. A view can restrict visible rows/columns, but its privilege and execution rules must support that restriction.
Inference control concerns learning protected individual facts indirectly from allowed aggregate answers.
Releasing SUM for a group and SUM for the same group excluding one known person may disclose that person's value by subtraction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about locks?

options.label: A
options.text: Locks with large granularity are easier for the DBMS to administer.

options.label: B
options.text: Locks with small granularity cause more conflicts.

options.label: C
options.text: Locks with large granularity produce fewer details for the DBMS to track.

options.label: D
options.text: Locks may have a table-level granularity.

options.label: E
options.text: Locks may have a database-level granularity.

questions.hint: Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 17

answer.text: Locks with small granularity cause more conflicts.
answer.explanation: Fine granularity raises concurrency, whereas coarse granularity locks more data with fewer lock entries. Thus the claim that smaller units cause more conflicts reverses the tradeoff.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A single coarse lock can replace many fine locks and reduce management work. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Fine units allow more independent access, so this is the false claim. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Coarse locks reduce the number of entries tracked. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The file/relation granularity in the hierarchy permits table-level locking. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Entire-database locking is expressly listed. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

evidence.quote: Fine-grained row locks permit more independent operations but require tracking many locks. Coarse table/database locks simplify management but block unrelated rows and reduce concurrency. Intention locks advertise planned descendant locks in a hierarchy; escalation replaces many small locks with a coarser one. Small granularity does not inherently cause more logical conflicts. Choose granularity from contention and management overhead, not a universal rule.

answer.text: Serial schedule
answer.explanation: Consecutive execution of every transaction's operations is the definition of a serial schedule. Recoverability and cascadelessness instead constrain dependencies on commits.

choices.explanation: Cascading concerns dependent rollbacks, not contiguous execution. (PDF pp. 72, 71.)

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Cascadeless means reading only committed writes. (PDF pp. 72, 71.)

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: A listed definition does match, so None is wrong. (PDF pp. 72, 71.)

evidence.quote: A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions. Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read/read pairs do not conflict.
Recoverable means if Tj reads Ti's value, Tj cannot commit before Ti commits.
Cascadeless means a transaction reads only values written by committed transactions, avoiding cascading aborts.

other transactions in the system continue normally?
questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 25

answer.text: Starvation
answer.explanation: Starvation means indefinite postponement of a transaction while other transactions continue. It can result from repeated waiting or repeated victim selection without any waiting cycle. Deadlock instead involves a cycle of mutually blocked transactions. A checkpoint records recovery state, and the lock point in two-phase locking is the instant a transaction acquires its final lock. Neither is the name of indefinite unfair postponement, so A remains the unique answer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Correct: indefinite postponement while others proceed is starvation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Incorrect: deadlock requires a waiting cycle, which is not required for starvation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incorrect: a checkpoint records durable recovery state; it is not an indefinite waiting condition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: the lock point is the instant the transaction acquires its final lock in 2PL.

evidence.quote: Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.
The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained.
A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.

questions.stem: The atom constructor can represent the following basic atomic values except.
questions.hint: Classify the shape of a value separately from an operation that creates an instance.
sources: Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 34

answer.text: Array is not an atom constructor.
answer.explanation: ADB04 lists integer, real, Boolean and string as examples of basic atomic values. An array instead supplies indexed positions and is a collection constructor, even when a programming variable holds it as one value. Consequently integers, reals and strings fit the atom category while an array is the requested exception.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An integer is explicitly listed as a basic atomic value.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A real number is explicitly included among atomic values.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A string is a basic atomic value under the object-model convention used here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An array contains indexed positions and is a collection constructor rather than an atomic one.

evidence.quote: In a common object model, an object is described by (OID,type constructor,state). An atom is one basic value, such as an integer, real, Boolean or string. A tuple constructor groups named component values into one structured record, such as (Street:'A',City:'B'). It is not a collection of records.
An array is not an atomic constructor merely because stored as one programming variable.
A set is an unordered collection without duplicates; a bag allows duplicates; a list has order; an array provides indexed positions.

questions.stem: A system crashes again during ARIES recovery. Durable WAL, pageLSNs and compensation log records survive; storage is intact. No checkpoints were taken. Which statement correctly describes the second restart?

options.label: A
options.text: The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again

options.label: C
options.text: Durable compensation records and pageLSNs preserve recovery progress, so already-installed actions can be skipped or safely redone as required.

questions.hint: Trace durable recovery metadata and what progress survives a second crash.
sources: Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 53

answer.text: C. Durable compensation records and pageLSNs preserve recovery progress, so already-installed actions can be skipped or safely redone as required.
answer.explanation: ARIES records recovery progress in durable metadata. PageLSNs help determine whether a redo action is already installed, and compensation records preserve undo progress and its continuation. A second restart can therefore recover safely without assuming that the same undo and redo work lists recur. Lack of checkpoints may increase scanning work, but it does not erase this progress or make further recovery impossible.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Durable progress can change the required work, so identical lists are not guaranteed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Restartable recovery does not make inconsistency inevitable.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: PageLSNs and durable CLRs support safe continuation after repeated crashes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: ARIES can restart using surviving durable recovery metadata.

evidence.quote: ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table. Analysis reconstructs active/loser transactions and dirty-page information. Redo repeats history, starting from the relevant earliest dirty-page update; pageLSNs help skip already-installed actions. Undo reverses loser transactions.
This makes recovery restartable: after a second crash, durable undo progress need not be undone again as if no progress occurred.
Compensation log records (CLRs) describe undo actions and their continuation information.

questions.stem: The rigorous two-phase locking protocol permits releasing all locks at the__________

options.label: D
options.text: Never in the life-time of transaction

questions.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
sources: Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 59

answer.text: At transaction end, on commit or abort.
answer.explanation: Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until commit or abort, unlike basic 2PL, which permits release in its shrinking phase. FDB-style early release would allow interference before completion and would not meet rigorous locking. The locks are eventually released at the transaction boundary, so never is also false.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Releasing locks at the beginning would not protect the transaction's later accesses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rigorous 2PL does not permit early release during ongoing transaction execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both shared and exclusive locks remain held until commit or abort ends the transaction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Locks are released at completion; the protocol does not hold them forever.

evidence.quote: Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort. Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until that point. Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock. It requires knowing the lock set and can reduce concurrency. Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.

questions.stem:
Let transaction T1 has obtained a shared mode lock S on data item Y and transaction T2 has
obtained an exclusive lock X on data item Z , according to the above statement which one is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: T1 can read Y but cannot write Y

options.label: B
options.text: T2 can read Z but cannot write Z

options.label: C
options.text: T1 can read Z but cannot write Z

options.label: D
options.text: T2 can read and write item Y

questions.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
sources: Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 67

answer.text: T1 can read Y but cannot write Y
answer.explanation: Shared locks permit reads but not updates. Exclusive locks permit both reading and updating while excluding other transactions' locks on that item.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: T1's shared lock authorizes reading Y, not writing it. (PDF pp. 82, 83.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: T2's exclusive lock permits both read and update of Z. (PDF pp. 82, 83.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: T1 cannot read Z while another transaction holds its exclusive lock. (PDF pp. 82, 83.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: T2 cannot obtain an exclusive write lock on Y while T1 holds its shared lock. (PDF pp. 82, 83.)

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks.
One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.

questions.stem: Which claim about deadlock prevention and starvation is false?

options.label: B
options.text: Wound–wait guarantees starvation freedom regardless of restart priorities or scheduling fairness

options.label: C
options.text: Deadlock can be prevented by wait-die

options.label: D
options.text: Some deadlock-prevention methods may cause starvation

questions.hint: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.
sources: Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 84

answer.text: Wound–wait guarantees starvation freedom regardless of restart priorities or scheduling fairness
answer.explanation: Deadlock freedom does not itself guarantee that each transaction eventually completes. Wound–wait uses transaction age to decide whether a requester waits or aborts a younger holder, but a starvation-freedom argument also needs appropriate restart priorities, fair scheduling and holders that eventually finish. Its unconditional guarantee in B is therefore false. Conservative 2PL can postpone a transaction indefinitely under unfair admission, and wait–die prevents waiting cycles. Some prevention policies can cause repeated waiting or victimization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: True: conservative 2PL prevents cycles but does not by itself guarantee fair admission.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct selection: the unconditional starvation-freedom claim omits necessary progress and priority assumptions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: True: wait–die is a timestamp-based deadlock-prevention policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: True: preventing deadlock can still leave a transaction repeatedly postponed or aborted.

evidence.quote: Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive. Starvation avoidance additionally assumes holders eventually finish and scheduling is fair.

Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.

questions.stem: Concurrency control in DBMS is important for which of the following reasons?

options.label: A
options.text: To ensure data integrity when updates occur to the database in a single user environment

options.label: B
options.text: To ensure data integrity when reads occur to the database in a single user environment

options.label: C
options.text: To ensure data integrity when updates occur to the database in a multi user environment

options.label: D
options.text: To ensure data integrity when reads occur to the database in a multi user environment

questions.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
sources: Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 85

answer.text: To ensure data integrity when updates occur to the database in a multi user environment
answer.explanation: Concurrency control preserves consistency when multiple users' updates interleave and conflict. Read-only sharing alone does not cause lost updates; the intended scenario is a multiuser system with updates.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Single-user updates lack concurrent intertransaction conflicts. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Single-user reads do not create the cited conflicts. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiuser updates can create read/write and write/write conflicts requiring scheduling. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reads can be involved when others update, but reads alone do not capture the source's motivating condition. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

evidence.quote: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.
Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.
Read/read pairs do not conflict.

questions.stem: A lock wait-for graph may contain several independent deadlock cycles. Which termination methods guarantee eliminating all deadlock cycles? Assume each aborted transaction is undone and releases its locks. Select all that apply. 'Half' and 'single' mean arbitrary selections without a repeated cycle check.

options.label: B
options.text: Abort half of the deadlocked transaction

options.label: D
options.text: Aborting one transaction at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated

questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 93

answer.text: A. Abort all deadlocked transaction; D. Aborting one transaction at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated
answer.explanation: Aborting all deadlocked transactions removes every participating wait, although it wastes work. A more selective complete method aborts a suitable victim, releases its locks and repeats until no cycles remain. An arbitrary half of the participants can leave a cycle intact, and one arbitrary victim may resolve only one of several independent cycles. The guarantee therefore applies to A and D.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Removing all deadlocked participants eliminates all their cycles.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An arbitrary half may miss an entire remaining cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One victim need not break other independent cycles.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Repeated victim selection and graph checking continues until every cycle is gone.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp.
Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote:
⚫ What causes a Transaction to fail
1. A computer failure (system crash):
A hardware or software error occurs in the computer system during transaction execution. If
the hardware crashes, the contents of the computer‘s internal memory may be lost.
2. A transaction or system error:
Some operation in the transaction may cause it to fail, such as integer overflow or division by
zero. Transaction failure may also occur because of erroneous parameter values or because of a
logical programming error. In addition, the user may interrupt the transaction during its
execution.
3. Exception conditions detected by the transaction:
◦ Certain conditions forces cancellation of the transaction.
◦ For example, data for the transaction may not be found. such as insufficient
account balance in a banking database, may cause a transaction, such as a fund
withdrawal from that account, to be canceled.
4. Concurrency control enforcement:
The concurrency control method may decide to abort the transaction, to be restarted later,
because it violates serializability or because several transactions are in a state of deadlock (see
Chapter 2).
5. Disk failure:
Some disk blocks may lose their data because of a read or write malfunction or because of a
disk read/write head crash. This may happen during a read or a write operation of the transaction.
6. Physical problems and catastrophes:
This refers to an endless list of problems that includes power or air-conditioning failure, fire,
theft, overwriting disks or tapes by mistake

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote:
◦ Deferred Update:
 All transaction updates are recorded in the local workspace (cache)
 All modified data items in the cache is then written after a transaction ends
its execution or after a fixed number of transactions have completed their
execution.
 During commit the updates are first recorded on the log and then on the
database
 If a transaction fails before reaching its commit point undo is not needed
because it didn‘t change the database yet
 If a transaction fails after commit (writing on the log) but before finishing
saving to the data base redoing is needed from the log
◦ Immediate Update:
 As soon as a data item is modified in cache, the disk copy is updated.
 These update are first recorded on the log and on the disk by force writing,
before the database is updated
 If a transaction fails after recording some change to the database but

questions.stem: Which listed policy prevents lock-wait deadlock without comparing transaction-age timestamps? Here 'wait-wait' means allowing every conflicting request to wait with no ordering or cycle restriction.
questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · Question 14-1
National Computer Science Exit Exam · Question 100
National Computer Science Exit Exam
MOE Computer Science Exit Exam
Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 63

answer.text: No-wait
answer.explanation: No-wait aborts immediately when a lock request conflicts, so transactions cannot form a lock-wait cycle and no age comparison is needed. Wait–die and wound–wait use relative transaction ages to decide who waits or aborts. Under the explicitly defined wait-wait alternative, every conflicting request may wait without a cycle-prevention restriction, so a transaction can hold one item while waiting for another in a cycle. That alternative therefore fails the deadlock-prevention requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect: unrestricted waiting permits a hold-and-wait cycle, so this defined policy does not prevent deadlock.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct: immediate abort on a conflicting request prevents lock waits without comparing ages.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incorrect: wound–wait compares requester and holder ages to choose waiting or aborting a younger holder.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: wait–die compares ages to choose whether the requester waits or aborts.

evidence.quote: Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.

A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote:
 Transaction Timestamp( TS(T) )
− We can prevent deadlocks by giving each transaction a priority and
ensuring that lower priority transactions are not allowed to wait for
higher priority transactions (or vice versa ).
− One way to assign priorities is to give each transaction a timestamp when
it starts up.
− it is a unique identifier given to each transaction based on time in which
it is started. i.e if T1 starts before T2 , TS(T1)<TS(T2)
− The lower the timestamp, the higher the transaction's priority, that is, the
oldest transaction has the highest priority.
− If a transaction Ti requests a lock and transaction Tj holds a conflicting
lock, the lock manager can use one of the following two policies: Wait-
die & Wound-wait
⚫ Wait-die
◦ If Ti has higher priority, it is allowed to wait; otherwise it is aborted.
◦ An older transaction is allowed to wait on a younger transaction.
◦ A younger transaction requesting an item held by an older transaction is aborted
◦ If TS(Ti) < TS(Tj), then (Ti older than Tj)Ti is allowed to wait.
◦ Otherwise (Ti younger than Tj)Abort Ti (Ti dies) and restart it later with the same
timestamp
T1(ts =10): M is locked , K is requested
T2 (ts =20): K is locked, Z is requested

module_refs.quote:
• Wound-wait
– The opposite of wait-die
– If Ti has higher priority, abort Tj; otherwise Ti waits.
– A younger transaction is allowed to wait on an older one
– An older transaction requesting an item held by a younger transaction preempts
the younger transaction by aborting it.
– If TS(Ti) < TS(Tj), then (Ti older than Tj),Abort Tj (Ti wounds Tj) and restart Tj

One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy. No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

Row-oriented storage instead groups each record's fields. Hierarchical and network models are logical representation alternatives rather than the physical column-oriented layout requested by the stem. A warehouse integrates data for historical analysis, often through extraction, transformation and loading. These are workload tendencies: OLTP can retain history and warehouses can be updated.
Columnar storage groups values by column, reducing unnecessary column reads and aiding compression in scans; row-oriented storage groups each record's fields.

questions.stem: An online game wants extra read copies of player reference data near regional users while retaining the same logical data. Which concept specifically creates those additional copies, rather than dividing the only copy into fragments or choosing a model family?

answer.text: A. Replication
answer.explanation: Replication creates additional copies of selected data and can improve read locality by placing them near users. That directly satisfies the specified regional read-copy requirement. Distribution is the broader arrangement across sites, partitioning divides data into fragments, and NoSQL names a family of data models. Neither the broader architecture nor a model label specifically says that extra copies are created.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replication creates the required regional read copies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NoSQL selects a model family and does not itself create copies.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Distribution is broader than the requested copy-creation policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Partitioning divides data; by itself it creates no spare copy.

evidence.quote: Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.
Partitioning improves locality and parallelism but alone creates no spare copy.
Flexible schema does not mean no schema rules, and NoSQL does not imply no transactions.

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote:
6.1 Distributed Database Concepts
 A transaction can be executed by multiple networked computers in a unified manner.
 A distributed database (DDB) processes Unit of execution (a transaction) in a
distributed manner.
 A distributed database (DDB) can be defined as :
– A collection of multiple logically related database distributed over a computer
network, and a distributed database management system as a software system that
manages a distributed database while making the distribution transparent to the
user.
– The physical placement of data (files, relations, etc.) which is not known to the
user (distribution transparency).

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote:
6.2 Data Replication and Fragmentation: Distributed data storage
 There are two approaches to store the relation in the distributed database : Replication
and Fragmentation
I. Data Replication
 The system maintain several identical copies of the relation & store each copy at a
different site
 In general it enhance the performance of read operation and increase the
availability of data to read only transaction. However, update transactions incur
greater overhead
II. Data Fragmentation
– Split a relation into logically related and correct parts.
– The main reasons for fragmenting a relation are
• Efficiency- data that is not needed by the local applications is not stored
• Parallelism – a transaction can be divided into several subqueries that
operate on fragments which will increase the degree of concurrency
– but reconstruction of the whole relation will require accessing data from all sites
containing part of the relation

answer.text: C. To group database operations into one logical unit of work
answer.explanation: A transaction groups database operations into one logical unit of work. The DBMS supports its atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability requirements, including controlled interference with concurrent transactions. Grouping is the defining concept, rather than query tuning, access authorization or schema construction. Read-only work can also form a transaction, so the definition is not limited to operations that change stored data.

choices.label: B

questions.stem: In the object-oriented model, an object is defined as:

options.label: C
options.text: A primary key in a database

questions.hint: Distinguish an object instance from its class, attribute values and persistent identity.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 185

answer.text: An instance of a class.
answer.explanation: ADB01 explicitly distinguishes a class specification from each object instantiated from it. A class defines available attributes and operations, while an object is one individual instance with identity, state and behavior. A collection of attributes omits identity and behavior; a key or an intertable relationship belongs to a different relational description.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An object is an individual instance of a class with its own identity and state.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Attributes describe state but omit the identity and behavior that also characterize an object.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A database primary key is an identifier constraint, not the definition of an object instance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A relationship between tables is a relational association rather than an object instance.

evidence.quote: An object combines identity, state and behavior. A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance. The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime. Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity.
Complex CAD or multimedia structures can suit an object model, but many-to-many relationships alone do not require abandoning relational design.
An object-relational DBMS extends a relational system with richer types; ORM maps programming objects into relational tables.

questions.stem: In the object-oriented model, encapsulation refers to:

options.label: B
options.text: Hiding the internal details of an object

sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 186

answer.text: Hiding and controlling access to internal object details.
answer.explanation: ADB02 describes encapsulation as grouping state with operations and controlling access to implementation details. A withdrawal method can enforce rules while hiding storage. B states the relevant information-hiding aspect. Combining classes, associating objects and defining subtype hierarchies are distinct activities; none describes the encapsulation boundary around an object's state and operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation groups an object's state and operations, not multiple classes into one entity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Encapsulation controls access to the internal representation behind the object's operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Links between objects are associations rather than encapsulation itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Superclass/subclass structure concerns inheritance rather than information-hiding boundaries.

evidence.quote: Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details. Account.withdraw(amount) can enforce a balance rule while hiding its storage. Abstraction presents the relevant contract—what withdrawal does—without exposing how it is implemented. These ideas overlap in information hiding, but combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation.
A class defines structure and behavior; an attribute describes state; a method implements an operation.
It is different from inheritance, which means an is-a relationship between types.

answer.text: Inherit applicable attributes and behavior from a superclass.
answer.explanation: ADB03 defines inheritance as deriving a subtype from a superclass and reusing its applicable attributes and behavior. B captures that idea. It does not inherently require multiple parents, dynamically create objects, or merely link unrelated objects. Those alternatives concern particular inheritance forms, instantiation or association rather than the general meaning of inheritance.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dynamic object creation is instantiation, not the capability defined by inheritance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Relationships between separate objects are associations rather than the is-a subtype relationship.

questions.stem:
Which concept in the object-oriented model allows different classes to share the same
method name but with different implementations?
questions.hint: Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 188

answer.text: Polymorphism.
answer.explanation: ADB03 illustrates Shape.area dispatching to Circle.area or Rectangle.area according to the actual object. The common operation name has different compatible implementations, which is polymorphism. Inheritance can provide the subtype structure used by that mechanism, but is not itself the runtime dispatch behavior. Abstraction and encapsulation concern contracts and implementation access instead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Polymorphism lets the same interface operation invoke different implementations for compatible object types.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes a relevant contract rather than selecting among differing method implementations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Encapsulation controls internal access rather than providing type-dependent method dispatch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance supplies a structural subtype relation; polymorphism describes the differing implementations through a common interface.

evidence.quote: Subtype polymorphism lets a superclass/interface reference denote objects of different compatible subclasses. The same operation can dispatch to different implementations: Shape.area() calls Circle.area() or Rectangle.area() according to the actual object. This is not arbitrary conversion of an object into an unrelated class, nor dynamic class mutation. Inheritance establishes a subtype relationship; polymorphism uses that relationship through a common interface. Distinguish inheritance as a structural relationship from polymorphism as a use of that relationship at runtime.

choices.label: D

questions.stem: The object-oriented model supports the concept of association, which represents:

answer.text: Links and interactions between objects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Having similar attributes does not itself define an association between particular objects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Associations link objects and support their interactions or collaboration through references.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Association represents relationships rather than duplicated copies of the same database facts.

undoing the effects of incomplete or failed transactions?

answer.text: Rollback recovery
answer.explanation: Undo restores before images and removes after images; failed transactions that updated the database must roll back (p.107). This directly answers the specific action, although undo may be one phase of broader crash recovery.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Rollback is the direct undo operation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Redo restores after images instead.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Checkpoints synchronize database and log; they do not name the undo action.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A restart can include undo, but is broader than the requested failed-transaction reversal.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.
Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.
Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.

state of the database and transaction logs?
questions.hint: Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 197

answer.text: Checkpoint recovery
answer.explanation: Checkpointing synchronizes database and log (p.105); its listed steps force modified buffers to disk, write a checkpoint record, and save the log (p.107). This is not necessarily a full database backup.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The named synchronization procedure matches.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Redo reapplies after images, not periodic synchronization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Rollback restores before images.

choices.explanation: Restart follows failure, whereas checkpoints are established during operation.

evidence.quote: A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk.

answer.text: Restart recovery

module_refs.title: Fundamental of Database Systems module
module_refs.quote:
⚫ What causes a Transaction to fail
1. A computer failure (system crash):
A hardware or software error occurs in the computer system during transaction execution. If
the hardware crashes, the contents of the computer‘s internal memory may be lost.
2. A transaction or system error:
Some operation in the transaction may cause it to fail, such as integer overflow or division by
zero. Transaction failure may also occur because of erroneous parameter values or because of a
logical programming error. In addition, the user may interrupt the transaction during its
execution.
3. Exception conditions detected by the transaction:
◦ Certain conditions forces cancellation of the transaction.
◦ For example, data for the transaction may not be found. such as insufficient
account balance in a banking database, may cause a transaction, such as a fund
withdrawal from that account, to be canceled.
4. Concurrency control enforcement:
The concurrency control method may decide to abort the transaction, to be restarted later,
because it violates serializability or because several transactions are in a state of deadlock (see
Chapter 2).
5. Disk failure:
Some disk blocks may lose their data because of a read or write malfunction or because of a
disk read/write head crash. This may happen during a read or a write operation of the transaction.
6. Physical problems and catastrophes:
This refers to an endless list of problems that includes power or air-conditioning failure, fire,
theft, overwriting disks or tapes by mistake

transaction manager when transactions begin and end, as well as information about the
expectations of the application.

options.label: B
options.text: A database system that uses multiple database management systems

options.label: C
options.text: A database system that supports multiple database schemas

sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 215

answer.text: A database system that is spread across multiple locations
answer.explanation: A DDB is multiple logically related databases distributed over a computer network, managed transparently (p.114). A captures the physical distribution; logical relatedness and coordinated management are implicit qualifications.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multiple locations captures the defining distribution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Different DBMS products are not required; homogeneous DDBs exist.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple schemas are not the physical distribution definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Storing distributed data is circular and omits the network/location criterion.

evidence.quote: A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system. A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces. Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction. Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization.
Distribution adds communication, coordination and security costs; a site outage can still make needed data unavailable if no usable replica exists.

 A transaction can be executed by multiple networked computers in a unified manner.
 A distributed database (DDB) processes Unit of execution (a transaction) in a
distributed manner.
 A distributed database (DDB) can be defined as :
– A collection of multiple logically related database distributed over a computer
network, and a distributed database management system as a software system that
manages a distributed database while making the distribution transparent to the
user.
– The physical placement of data (files, relations, etc.) which is not known to the
user (distribution transparency).

answer.text: It manages the distribution and retrieval of data across multiple sites.
answer.explanation: Distributed query processing compares moving source relations and results among sites, selecting the lower-transfer strategy (pp.120–121). B best captures distributed retrieval, understood as planning transfers for a query rather than deciding the physical database design.

choices.label: A

choices.explanation: Physical local storage management is not choosing distributed query strategies.

evidence.quote: Distributed processing decomposes a logical query, localizes referenced relations to fragments/replicas, chooses global placement/order and optimizes local subplans. answer.text: Standardization of database management systems across all sites
answer.explanation: Homogeneity is defined by using the same or compatible DBMS technology across sites. Schema compatibility, functioning network connections and replication can be useful design concerns, but none alone establishes that common DBMS technology. choices.explanation: Lazy replication propagates changes later and can expose stale reads or require conflict handling.

choices.explanation: Snapshot replication distributes a copy at intervals rather than necessarily sending each individual update.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incremental replication transfers changes and can coexist with a propagation-timing policy.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous distributed databases?
questions.hint: Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 1

answer.text: Homogeneous systems use compatible DBMS technology; heterogeneous systems integrate differing DBMSs, models, schemas or interfaces.
answer.explanation: ADB33 defines the distinction through compatibility of database technology and representation. Operating-system differences can occur but do not define heterogeneity. Homogeneous sites need not have identical schemas or automatic replication. Heterogeneous integration requires explicit mappings for names, types and semantics, rather than assuming that common connectivity alone reconciles their meanings.

evidence.quote: A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system. A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces. Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction. Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization.
ODBC and JDBC provide connectivity interfaces; they do not automatically solve semantic differences or create one distributed transaction.
Heterogeneous design must reconcile naming, types, units, identifiers, query capabilities and transaction semantics.

questions.stem: Why is data fragmentation useful in distributed databases?
questions.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 2

answer.text: Fragmentation improves locality, manageable placement and parallelism by splitting data across useful site boundaries.
answer.explanation: ADB36 splits rows with predicates and columns with projections while preserving reconstruction through unions or key joins. This can place frequently used data near its consumers and allow independent work on pieces. Correct fragments must preserve completeness and required disjointness. Fragmentation alone creates no spare copy, so losing the only site containing a fragment still makes it unavailable.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Partitioning improves locality and parallelism but alone creates no spare copy.
Losing the only site containing a fragment makes that fragment unavailable, even while other sites continue.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of two-phase locking (2PL) in concurrency control?
questions.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 3

answer.text: 2PL guarantees conflict serializability by separating lock acquisition from release.
answer.explanation: During the growing phase a transaction acquires or upgrades locks; after it releases any lock, the shrinking phase forbids acquiring new ones. For well-formed transactions this guarantees conflict serializability. Basic 2PL can still deadlock and permit cascading aborts, so strict or conservative variants add different protections. It is distinct from distributed two-phase commit.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort.

questions.stem: Why is write-ahead logging important for database recovery?
questions.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 4

answer.text: WAL makes recovery information durable before its changed data pages, enabling safe undo/redo after crashes.
answer.explanation: ADB27 requires needed update logs to reach stable storage before corresponding changed pages. A durable commit also forces required log records, including commit. Recovery can then use before-images for undo and after-images for redo if buffered data was lost. WAL orders durable writes; modifying an in-memory buffer before the log flush does not itself violate it.

evidence.quote: Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk. To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage. A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.
Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.
Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward.

questions.stem: How does a data warehouse differ from an operational database?
questions.hint: Distinguish operational transactions, analytical workloads and physical storage layout.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 5

answer.text: A warehouse integrates historical data for analysis; an operational database serves frequent business transactions.
answer.explanation: OLTP handles account updates and other frequent operational transactions, while OLAP scans and summarizes large datasets. A warehouse commonly integrates sources through extraction, transformation and loading for historical analysis. These are workload tendencies rather than absolute restrictions: operational databases may retain history, and warehouses may receive updates. Schema and storage choices should follow the actual workload.

evidence.quote: OLTP handles frequent operational transactions, such as account updates; OLAP scans and summarizes large datasets for analysis. A warehouse integrates data for historical analysis, often through extraction, transformation and loading. These are workload tendencies: OLTP can retain history and warehouses can be updated.

answer.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
answer.explanation: ADB06 names all four ACID properties and assigns distinct roles: all-or-none effects, preserved invariants, controlled interference and durable commits. Only A lists those names in the correct order. Accuracy, integrity, concurrency, data and availability are related database concepts but do not replace the letters of this established transaction acronym.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It lists the four ACID properties in the proper acronym order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Accuracy and Integrity replace Atomicity and Isolation, changing the defined acronym.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrency and Data incorrectly replace Consistency and Durability.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Availability is not the A in the ACID transaction acronym.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.

questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.

answer.text: Atomicity.
answer.explanation: The question specifies indivisibility of the transaction effects: partial success must not remain if the transaction fails. ADB06 assigns that guarantee to atomicity. Consistency concerns valid invariants, isolation controls interference, and durability protects already committed work. Those properties support correctness too, but none directly means all-or-none effects.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns preserving integrity rules rather than specifically making effects indivisible.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Isolation controls interactions between concurrent transactions rather than partial transaction application.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Atomicity applies every transaction effect together or discards the incomplete work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Durability protects committed effects after failure rather than defining all-or-none completion.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.

questions.stem: Account A = 5,000 Birr, Account B = 8,000 Birr. After transferring 750 Birr from A to B, which values maintain CONSISTENCY?
questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 3

answer.text: A = 4,250 Birr and B = 8,750 Birr.
answer.explanation: The requested transfer subtracts 750 from 5000 and adds 750 to 8000, giving 4250 and 8750. The invariant total remains 13000. questions.stem: A transaction that has started and is currently executing its operations is in which state?
questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 6

answer.text: Active.
answer.explanation: ADB06 defines Active as the state while transaction operations are executing. Partially committed follows completion of the last operation but precedes assured durable commitment. Committed means commitment succeeded, while Failed means execution encountered a failure. Merely starting and continuing its operations therefore places this transaction in Active.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Committed requires successful commitment, which has not occurred while operations are still executing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Partially committed follows the last operation rather than ordinary ongoing execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Active is the state during execution of the transaction operations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Failed requires an execution failure, which the stem does not report.

evidence.quote: Active means operations are executing. Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured. Committed means commitment succeeded. A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt. Active describes operations still running, while Aborted means rollback completed, so neither matches successful operations awaiting finalized commit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Active means operations are still executing, whereas the last operation has finished here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Partially committed means execution finished but durable commitment is not yet assured.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

answer.text: T is aborting/aborted and its transaction effects must be discarded.

questions.stem: The Isolation property of ACID ensures that concurrent transactions:

answer.text: Concurrent work is isolated from improper interference.
answer.explanation: ADB06 defines isolation as controlling interference between concurrent transactions. B captures logical independence under the specified isolation guarantee; it does not mean transactions literally use separate hardware or never wait. Isolation does not require identical reads, start-order commits or universal successful completion. Strong serializable isolation makes behavior equivalent to some serial order.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Isolation does not require all transactions to read identical values at the same time.

choices.label: B

questions.stem: In a simplified teaching sequence, write_item(X) updates a buffered page and then the buffer manager immediately flushes that page, after required WAL records are durable. What is the final physical step of this specified sequence?

answer.text: C. Store the updated buffer block back to disk
answer.explanation: After X's program value has been copied into the buffered page, the specified sequence completes by writing the changed page back to disk. That is C. In ordinary buffering this flush may be deferred, but the question explicitly includes it. Locating a page or reading its old value occurs before or separately from the final physical output, and copying into a program variable describes reading.

answer.text: Failed.
answer.explanation: ADB06 places a transaction in Failed when an error prevents successful execution. After rollback removes its effects it reaches Aborted. The stem reports the execution error but does not say rollback has completed, so Failed is the precise state. Partially committed follows successful final operation execution, not an error that prevents completion.

questions.stem: Transaction log records serve primarily for which purpose?

options.label: C
options.text: Enabling database recovery after failures by recording all changes

questions.hint: Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 13

answer.text: Enable recovery by recording the information needed to undo or redo changes.
answer.explanation: ADB07 records starts, updates, commits and aborts, with before-images for undo and after-images for redo. That makes recovery the primary purpose among the choices. Actual log formats may be physical or logical and need not record every read, so all changes should be understood as the change information required by the recovery design, not every operation indiscriminately.

choices.explanation: The primary log purpose here is recovery rather than speeding query execution.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

questions.stem: Which processing type uses multiple CPUs to execute different transactions simultaneously, achieving higher throughput?
questions.hint: Distinguish overlapping dependent operators, independent workers and reused cached objects.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 14

answer.text: Parallel processing.
answer.explanation: ADB22 distinguishes concurrency by interleaving on one CPU from actual simultaneous work on multiple cores. The stem explicitly uses multiple CPUs to execute different transactions at the same time, making Parallel the correct classification. Batch describes grouping work, and sequential processing performs work in order; neither guarantees the stated simultaneous execution.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Sequential processing does not execute different transactions simultaneously on multiple CPUs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Interleaving alternates execution and need not provide simultaneous CPU work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple CPUs working simultaneously provide parallel execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Batch describes grouped submission or handling, not necessarily simultaneous multi-CPU execution.

evidence.quote: Materialization stores an intermediate result before the next operator consumes it. Pipelining passes tuples as they become available, overlapping producer and consumer work and reducing temporary I/O. A sort is normally blocking; a hash join must build its hash table before probing can output, though later probe/output can stream. Pipelining does not require separate CPUs.
Interleaving on one CPU is concurrency; simultaneous cores provide parallelism.
Parallel execution uses multiple workers, for example partitioned scans/joins, independent subplans or operator pipelines.

questions.stem: Why are transactions important in database systems?

options.label: B
options.text: They ensure the database remains consistent and reliable through ACID properties

options.label: C
options.text: They allow the database to store more data

options.label: D
options.text: They simplify the SQL syntax for users
