answer.text: Transactions support consistent, reliable work through ACID guarantees.
answer.explanation: ADB06 groups operations into a logical unit with all-or-none effects, invariant preservation, isolation and durable commits. These guarantees support consistent and reliable database behavior when application logic is correct. They do not inherently speed queries, expand storage capacity or simplify syntax. In particular a DBMS cannot make an incorrect business operation consistent merely by wrapping it in a transaction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transactions can add coordination costs and do not inherently make queries faster.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ACID guarantees support valid and recoverable logical work, provided business logic is correct.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transaction semantics do not increase the database's physical storage capacity.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Grouping work atomically does not inherently simplify the SQL language for users.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.

questions.stem: T1 reads balance=$500 and adds $100, planning to write $600. T2 reads the same $500, adds $200, and writes $700. T1 then writes $600. What problem occurred?
questions.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 16

answer.text: Lost update: T1 overwrites T2’s increment with its stale calculation.
answer.explanation: Both transactions read 500. T2 writes 700 after adding 200, but T1 then writes its previously computed 600, erasing T2’s increment. A serial execution would produce 800. This matches the lost-update trace in ADB08; no waiting cycle or aggregate calculation is described, and reading an uncommitted value is not the stated cause.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Neither transaction is described as reading the other's uncommitted write.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: T1's stale write of 600 overwrites T2's added 200; the correct combined result is 800.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No aggregate over mutually inconsistent versions is being calculated.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No circular waiting or blocked resource requests are present.

evidence.quote: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.
Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X.
Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200.

questions.stem: A dirty read occurs when transaction T1 reads data that:

options.label: A
options.text: T1 itself wrote earlier in the same transaction

options.label: B
options.text: T2 modified but has NOT yet committed, and T2 may later abort

options.label: C
options.text: Was permanently deleted from the database

options.label: D
options.text: Was last read more than one hour ago

questions.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 17

answer.text: Read another transaction’s uncommitted modification.
answer.explanation: ADB08 defines dirty read as consuming a value written by an uncommitted other transaction. If that writer aborts, the dependent read used a value that should not survive. Reading one’s own changes is allowed and is not this anomaly; the age of a value or a completed permanent deletion does not define dirty reading.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reading changes made earlier by the same transaction is not a dirty read.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The read depends on T2's uncommitted update, which may later need undo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Permanent deletion is not the defining uncommitted-value dependency.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Elapsed time since a read does not determine whether the writer committed.

Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.

questions.stem: Which lock type allows MULTIPLE transactions to simultaneously READ a data item?
questions.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 18

answer.text: Shared lock.
answer.explanation: ADB11 states that a shared lock permits reading and multiple shared holders can coexist on the same item. Exclusive/write locks conflict with another transaction’s shared or exclusive lock on that item. Thus shared locking provides the requested concurrent-reader behavior. A generic binary locked/unlocked label does not establish shared-reader compatibility in the supplied model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An exclusive lock conflicts with other transactions' read locks on the same item.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A write/exclusive lock does not grant multiple independent readers the requested shared ownership.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks, permitting multiple readers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The binary label does not provide the explicit S/S compatibility defined in the note.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
Shared/exclusive locking adds modes so multiple shared readers can coexist while incompatible exclusive access is excluded.
One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.

questions.stem: In Two-Phase Locking (2PL), a transaction can acquire new locks ONLY during which phase?
questions.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 19

answer.text: Growing phase.
answer.explanation: Basic 2PL separates acquiring/upgrading locks from releasing/downgrading them. ADB12 permits acquisition only in the growing phase; after any release, no new lock may be acquired. Termination is a transaction boundary and validation belongs to a different control approach. The growing/shrinking rule is what distinguishes 2PL from unrestricted use of locks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The shrinking phase releases or downgrades locks and forbids new acquisitions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Termination is not the 2PL phase in which new locks are acquired.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Growing permits acquiring and upgrading locks before any release begins.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Validation is an optimistic-control stage, not the lock-acquisition phase of 2PL.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.

questions.stem: What does Two-Phase Locking (2PL) guarantee that locking alone does NOT guarantee?

Basic 2PL can still deadlock and may permit cascading aborts, so it does not guarantee successful completion. Nor does serializability require every read to observe the latest wall-clock update.

choices.explanation: Basic 2PL can deadlock, so deadlock freedom is not its general guarantee.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The phase discipline guarantees conflict-serializable schedules for well-formed transactions.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Serializability does not require every read to see the newest wall-clock version.

The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.

questions.stem: What is a deadlock in database systems?

options.label: A
options.text: A transaction that executes too slowly

options.label: B
options.text: A circular wait where each transaction holds a resource another needs, and none can proceed

options.label: C
options.text: A type of hardware failure causing data loss

options.label: D
options.text: When a transaction violates the ACID consistency property

questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 21

answer.text: A circular wait among transactions holding resources needed by others.
answer.explanation: ADB13 defines deadlock through a waiting cycle: each participant holds a resource another needs, so none can advance without an intervention. Slow work alone can still make progress and is not deadlock. Hardware loss and consistency violations are distinct problems that do not require a resource-wait cycle.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A slow transaction may still make progress and need not participate in a wait cycle.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Circular hold-and-wait prevents the involved transactions from progressing without intervention.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hardware failure is a different failure category and does not define a lock wait cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A consistency violation concerns invalid data states rather than necessarily circular waiting.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.
Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts.

options.label: B

options.label: D

answer.text: Abort the younger requester; retry with its original timestamp.
answer.explanation: The requester is younger and the resource holder older. ADB14 says wait–die permits an older requester to wait but aborts a younger requester needing an older holder. C therefore gives the correct action. Restart should retain the original timestamp to improve relative priority; immediately aborted does not require an immediate successful retry or resource grant.

choices.explanation: Wait–die does not let the younger requester abort the older holder.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In wait–die, the younger requester dies rather than waiting for the older holder.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The younger requester is aborted and may restart using its original timestamp.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The older holder retains priority; the younger requester does not receive the resource immediately.

evidence.quote: A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.

questions.stem: In the Wound-Wait strategy, when an OLDER transaction needs a resource held by a YOUNGER transaction:

options.label: A
options.text: The older transaction waits for the younger

options.label: B
options.text: The older transaction wounds (aborts) the younger transaction

questions.hint: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 23

answer.text: The older requester aborts the younger holder.
answer.explanation: ADB14 distinguishes wound–wait from wait–die: an older requester wounds the younger holder, while a younger requester waits for an older holder. Here the requester is explicitly older, so B applies. The rule prevents waiting cycles through age-based action; it does not require detecting an existing deadlock first or aborting both participants.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under wound–wait.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The older requester causes the younger resource holder to abort and release its lock.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The protocol aborts the younger holder, not both transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is a prevention action based on ages, not a requirement to run cycle detection first.

evidence.quote: A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.
A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model.
A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp.

questions.stem: Optimistic concurrency control is BEST suited for environments where:

options.label: A
options.text: Transactions frequently write to the same data items

options.label: B
options.text: Write operations always conflict with read operations

options.label: C
options.text: Conflicts between transactions are rare (read-heavy workloads)

options.label: D
options.text: All transactions must complete in strict timestamp order

questions.hint: Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 24

answer.text: Conflicts between transactions are rare (read-heavy workloads)
answer.explanation: Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions read and compute privately, then validates overlapping read/write activity before publishing changes. When conflicts are rare, most work can commit without being discarded. Frequent competing writes or persistent read/write conflicts instead lead to costly retries. Strict timestamp completion describes a separate ordering constraint; it does not supply the low-conflict condition that makes optimistic execution suitable. Read-heavy activity is useful here only insofar as actual conflicts remain uncommon.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect: frequent competing writes cause validation failures and discarded work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Incorrect: persistent read/write conflicts increase retry costs rather than favoring optimistic execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Correct: rare conflicts allow most private work to validate and commit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: a required completion order does not imply low contention; optimistic suitability depends on conflicts and retry cost.

evidence.quote: Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries. It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts.

questions.stem: Lock upgrade refers to changing a lock from:
questions.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 25

answer.text: Shared → Exclusive.
answer.explanation: ADB11 explicitly names S→X an upgrade and X→S a downgrade. The stronger exclusive lock permits writing and can be granted only after conflicting other holders leave. Acquiring a new shared lock is initial acquisition rather than conversion, while releasing an exclusive lock is unlocking. Thus B alone names a lock upgrade.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-shared weakens permissions and is a downgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the held lock to permit writing, subject to compatibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No-lock-to-shared is initial acquisition, not conversion of an already held lock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-no-lock is release rather than upgrade.

evidence.quote: A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks. S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave. X→S is a downgrade. The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests. One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy. No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

questions.stem: Which trace demonstrates an incorrect-summary anomaly? The intended anomaly is a mixed-version aggregate, distinct from a nonrepeatable read.

options.label: A
options.text: Two transactions both delete the same record simultaneously

options.label: B
options.text: Initially A=B=100. During T2's transfer of 10 from A to B, T1 sums old A=100 and new B=110, returning 210 although the total-balance invariant is 200.

options.label: C
options.text: A transaction reads uncommitted data from another transaction

options.label: D
options.text: A transaction fails to acquire all necessary locks

questions.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 26

answer.text: B. Initially A=B=100. During T2's transfer of 10 from A to B, T1 sums old A=100 and new B=110, returning 210 although the total-balance invariant is 200.
answer.explanation: The transfer preserves the total balance at 200, but T1 combines the pre-transfer debit balance with the post-transfer credit balance. Its computed 100+110=210 is not a valid summary of a consistent state. This is an incorrect-summary anomaly. Dirty reading is defined by an uncommitted dependency, and lock failure or simultaneous deletion alone does not establish this mixed aggregate.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Concurrent deletion alone does not specify an inconsistent aggregate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The mixed old/new balances yield 210 instead of the invariant 200.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reading another transaction's uncommitted value defines a dirty read.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Failure to acquire locks concerns scheduling rather than this aggregate result.

evidence.quote: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.
Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200.
A single committed update from B=20 to B=50 does not alone prove an invalid summary of 90.

questions.stem: Starvation in a database system occurs when:

options.label: A
options.text: A transaction consumes excessive memory resources

options.label: B
options.text: A transaction is repeatedly bypassed by higher-priority transactions and never executes

options.label: C
options.text: A deadlock persists longer than the timeout period

options.label: D
options.text: The transaction log becomes completely full

questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 27

answer.text: Indefinite postponement while other transactions keep progressing.
answer.explanation: ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without requiring any waiting cycle. Repeatedly favoring higher-priority work can prevent a transaction from executing, matching B. Memory consumption, a full log or a long deadlock are different resource/failure conditions; none alone defines the fairness failure of starvation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Excessive memory use is a resource problem rather than the definition of indefinite postponement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated bypass by other transactions can indefinitely postpone this transaction while work continues.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle; starvation can occur without one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A full log can block work but does not itself define unfair indefinite postponement.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle.
Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.

questions.stem: Which concurrency control technique assigns a unique start-time value to each transaction and uses this to order execution and resolve conflicts?
questions.hint: Compare the transaction timestamp with the item's recorded read and write timestamps.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 28

answer.text: Timestamp-based concurrency control.
answer.explanation: ADB15 assigns TS(T) to each transaction and compares it with item read_TS and write_TS values. Those tests reject operations that would violate timestamp order, so C matches the start-time ordering technique. 2PL orders locking, optimistic control validates private work, and shadow paging is a recovery/storage technique rather than this conflict-ordering protocol.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 2PL orders lock acquisition and release rather than defining the timestamp validity tests.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves page versions for recovery rather than ordering concurrent transaction operations by timestamp.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Timestamp ordering compares transaction timestamps with item read/write timestamps to resolve conflicts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Optimistic control validates private read/write work rather than being defined by these timestamp-order tests.

evidence.quote: Assign each transaction TS(T). For item X track read_TS(X), the largest timestamp of a successful reader, and write_TS(X), that of its latest successful writer. A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS. A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS. These tests preserve timestamp order.
Multiversion control keeps versions so a reader can use an appropriate snapshot.
Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers.

questions.stem: A well-formed transaction must follow which rule regarding locking?

options.label: A
options.text: Lock all items at the end of the transaction

options.label: B
options.text: Lock a data item BEFORE reading or writing it

options.label: C
options.text: Lock items only when modifying them, not when reading

options.label: D
options.text: Acquire all locks in alphabetical order by item name

questions.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 29

answer.text: Acquire the appropriate lock before accessing the item.
answer.explanation: ADB11 requires ownership of an appropriate lock before access and permits releasing only one’s own locks. Reads therefore need shared or suitable stronger locks in this basic model; writes need exclusive ownership. Alphabetical acquisition may be a separate prevention convention, but it is not the general well-formedness rule and locks cannot be postponed until after access.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locking only at the end leaves the earlier accesses unprotected.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A well-formed transaction holds an appropriate lock before reading or writing an item.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Basic lock-based access also requires an appropriate read lock, not only locks for writes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A fixed resource order can help prevention, but alphabetical order is not the general well-formedness definition.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks.
Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.

questions.stem: Lock timeout as a deadlock solution works by:

options.label: A
options.text: Detecting cycles in the wait-for graph

options.label: B
options.text: Building a priority queue of all waiting transactions

options.label: C
options.text: Automatically aborting a transaction that has waited too long for a lock

options.label: D
options.text: Locking all required data items before execution begins

questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 30

answer.text: Abort a transaction after its lock wait exceeds the timeout.
answer.explanation: ADB13 describes timeout as aborting long waits, while warning it may mistake slow progress for deadlock. C directly states that mechanism. Detecting cycles is a different method; acquiring all needed locks first is conservative locking; a priority queue alone neither defines a timeout nor guarantees elimination of waiting cycles.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Cycle detection is graph-based deadlock detection rather than a wait-duration timeout.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A priority queue alone does not enforce the stated wait-duration abort policy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The policy aborts work whose lock wait exceeds the chosen threshold.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Obtaining all locks before execution is conservative locking, not timeout handling.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.
Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.

questions.stem: What are the three phases of query processing in the correct order?
questions.hint: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 31

answer.text: Parsing/translation → optimization → evaluation.
answer.explanation: ADB17 checks grammar and semantics, constructs a logical representation, chooses an equivalent efficient execution plan and evaluates it. B groups parsing and translation into the first phase and preserves that dependency order. Plans cannot sensibly be evaluated before construction and selection, and optimization does not precede understanding the query’s syntax and meaning.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Optimization cannot precede parsing and understanding the query in the stated pipeline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It preserves analysis/translation, plan optimization and then execution/evaluation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Evaluation cannot be the first phase before the query is represented and planned.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It executes before selecting the optimized plan, reversing optimization and evaluation.

evidence.quote: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.
Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.
DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence.

questions.stem: During query translation, SQL is typically converted into which internal representation for processing?
questions.hint: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 32

answer.text: Relational algebra expressions or a logical query tree.
answer.explanation: ADB17 states that translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. This allows equivalent rewrites and plan choice before physical execution. Machine code or bytecode may appear in particular execution implementations, but they are not the general logical translation target asked for here; a binary decision tree is also not the defined representation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Machine code is not the logical relational representation described for query translation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A binary decision tree is not the note's general query-algebra representation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Relational algebra expresses the logical operators that can be rewritten and optimized.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compressed bytecode is not the stated general logical query representation.

evidence.quote: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.
A query tree has base relations at leaves and operators at internal nodes; a query graph emphasizes relations and predicates.
A physical execution plan adds scan/index choices and algorithms.

questions.stem: The query optimizer's primary goal is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Ensure queries return results in sorted order

options.label: B
options.text: Find an execution plan that minimizes the overall cost of retrieving data

options.label: C
options.text: Maximize the number of indexes used in the query

options.label: D
options.text: Ensure all tables are accessed in the order written in SQL

questions.hint: Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 33

answer.text: Choose a low-cost equivalent execution plan.
answer.explanation: ADB19 estimates resource costs such as I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and communication for candidate plans. Optimization compares equivalent ways to return the same result and chooses a suitable low-cost strategy. It does not seek index count, force textual table order or impose sorting that the query never requested. The estimate need not prove a global real-world minimum.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Sorting is required only when query semantics need it, not as the universal optimizer goal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The optimizer seeks an efficient equivalent plan under the selected resource-cost model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: More indexes used does not necessarily mean lower cost or better execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Equivalent join reordering can reduce cost; SQL textual order need not dictate access order.

evidence.quote: A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions. Selection with fraction s predicts s×N rows. For non-NULL equijoin keys, a common estimate is |R|×|S|/max(V(R,k),V(S,k)), assuming uniform values and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain within the larger. Adjust counts for NULLs; if either non-NULL input is empty, the result is zero. Skew, correlations or incomplete domain overlap can invalidate this estimate; known disjoint domains give zero matches.
Avoid universal rules that joins always beat subqueries, functions can never use indexes or more indexes always improve performance.
Cost-based optimization estimates candidate plans instead of relying on rules alone.

questions.stem: In the textbook local rotating-disk cost model, data is not memory-resident and query execution is disk-bound; client/network and CPU costs are negligible by comparison. Which component dominates the estimated query cost?

options.label: B
options.text: Disk I/O time (seek time + transfer time)

questions.hint: Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 34

answer.text: B. Disk I/O time (seek time + transfer time)
answer.explanation: The specified disk-bound model estimates the cost of seeks and transferred blocks. Because CPU, memory-management and network costs are negligible by assumption, disk I/O dominates this query's estimated cost. This is a contextual model rather than a universal fact about all databases: memory-resident or distributed workloads can have different dominant resources. The answer follows the scenario's stated objective.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU cost is negligible in the specified model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Seek and transfer time dominate the stated disk-bound workload.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memory-management overhead is negligible here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Client/network cost is negligible in this local scenario.

evidence.quote: For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.

questions.stem: In the disk I/O cost formula Cost = (S x tS) + (B x tT), what does 'B' represent?
questions.hint: Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 35

answer.text: The number of transferred disk blocks.
answer.explanation: ADB19 computes disk cost as seeks times seek duration plus transferred blocks times per-block transfer time. Therefore B in the formula is a block count, making B×tT the total transfer time. Block size, buffer capacity and search-operation count are different quantities and would not have the units required by this expression.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Block size is bytes per block rather than the number multiplied by per-block transfer time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: B counts transferred blocks, so B×tT gives their total transfer time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Buffer-pool capacity is not the transferred-block count in this formula.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Binary-search operation count is not the disk-block transfer term.

evidence.quote: For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.

questions.stem: The UNDO operation in database recovery is used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Re-apply changes of committed transactions not yet written to disk

options.label: B
options.text: Create new checkpoint entries in the log

options.label: C
options.text: Reverse changes made by incomplete or aborted transactions

options.label: D
options.text: Transfer data from cache to permanent disk storage

questions.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 36

answer.text: Reverse incomplete or aborted transaction effects.
answer.explanation: ADB27 uses undo to restore before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing a transaction’s updates backward. This removes changes that must not survive. Reapplying committed changes is redo, checkpoint records bound recovery searches, and transferring dirty buffers to storage is page flushing. Only C describes undo rather than another recovery or storage operation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reapplying missing committed updates is redo rather than undo.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checkpoint creation records recovery state and is not reversal of incomplete effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Undo restores old values to remove incomplete or aborted transaction changes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Writing a buffer to disk is flushing rather than restoring before-images.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.
A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.
In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo.

questions.stem: The REDO operation in database recovery is used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Abort all active transactions found in the log

options.label: B
options.text: Reverse changes made by failed transactions

options.label: C
options.text: Re-apply changes of committed transactions not yet written to disk

options.label: D
options.text: Create shadow copies of database pages

questions.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 37

answer.text: Reapply required logged after-images, including committed changes missing from pages.
answer.explanation: ADB27 describes redo as installing logged after-images when necessary. In the simple teaching model it preserves committed work not yet on disk, matching C. ARIES may repeat history more broadly before loser undo, so C describes the ordinary purpose rather than every algorithm’s full phase. Aborting transactions and reversing failed changes are different actions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Aborting active transactions is not the operation of applying logged after-images.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reversing incomplete effects is undo rather than redo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Redo can restore committed changes whose data pages were not durable at the crash.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shadow-page creation is a separate copy-on-write technique rather than logged redo.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.
Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable.

questions.stem: What is the fundamental durable-write ordering rule of write-ahead logging? In B, 'actual data changes' means writing the corresponding changed data page to persistent storage, not modifying a volatile buffer.

options.label: A
options.text: Write data to disk before creating the log record

options.label: B
options.text: Log records must be written to stable storage BEFORE making the actual data changes

options.label: C
options.text: All transactions must commit before any log entries are written

options.label: D
options.text: Log records are written only after a system crash occurs

questions.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 38

answer.text: B. Log records must be written to stable storage BEFORE making the actual data changes
answer.explanation: WAL requires the recovery log for an update to reach stable storage before its corresponding changed page is written to disk. A volatile buffer may already contain the change, so this rule does not order every CPU assignment after a log flush. A reverses the required durable order; C and D postpone logs until too late to support recovery of earlier persistent changes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Data-before-log reverses WAL's required durable ordering.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: With the defined durable-write scope, the log reaches stable storage first.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Update logs may need to be durable before commit and before data flushing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Recovery requires logs that were durable before the crash.

evidence.quote: Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk. To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage. A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.
Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not.
Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.

questions.stem: In a simple quiescent checkpoint exercise, all transactions have completed and the required log/data pages are flushed at the checkpoint. How does that checkpoint reduce later recovery search work?

options.label: A
options.text: Preventing all types of hardware failures

options.label: B
options.text: Encrypting log records for faster access

options.label: C
options.text: Providing a known consistent state so recovery can start from there instead of the log beginning

options.label: D
options.text: Automatically committing all active transactions periodically

questions.hint: Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 39

answer.text: C. Providing a known consistent state so recovery can start from there instead of the log beginning
answer.explanation: The quiescent checkpoint supplies a durable boundary for the simplified exercise. With no active transaction spanning it and the required pages flushed, recovery need not scan all earlier history to redo those completed changes. C captures that bounded search. Checkpointing does not prevent hardware failure, gain its benefit from encryption or automatically commit active transactions. Fuzzy checkpoints require different starting-point qualifications.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Recording recovery state does not prevent hardware failures.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Encryption is not the mechanism reducing log-search work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The specified durable checkpoint bounds the history needed in this exercise.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Transactions have completed here; a checkpoint does not automatically commit active work.

evidence.quote: A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.
Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.
A checkpoint is neither a full backup nor an automatic commit of active transactions.

questions.stem: In deferred update (No-Undo) recovery, actual database modifications are written to disk:

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately as each SQL statement executes

options.label: B
options.text: Only AFTER the transaction successfully commits

options.label: C
options.text: When a checkpoint operation is triggered

options.label: D
options.text: At regular 5-minute intervals regardless of transaction state

questions.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 40

answer.text: After successful commit, in the deferred-update model.
answer.explanation: ADB29 keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database. Only committed effects may therefore be installed in its actual database pages, which is the property B expresses. This does not require every committed page to be flushed immediately. Checkpoints and periodic timers cannot independently authorize writing uncommitted changes while retaining the claimed No-Undo model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Immediate per-statement persistent writes can expose uncommitted effects and do not define deferred update.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The model does not install uncommitted effects in the persistent database; committed changes can be written later.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A checkpoint alone does not make an uncommitted transaction eligible for persistent installation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A fixed timer cannot ignore transaction commit status while preserving deferred-update semantics.

evidence.quote: Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.
Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable.

questions.stem: Shadow paging recovery technique preserves the original database pages by:

options.label: A
options.text: Creating a backup on a separate server

options.label: B
options.text: Writing all modifications to NEW shadow pages, keeping originals intact until commit

options.label: D
options.text: Storing pages in sorted order for faster access

questions.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 41

answer.text: Write changed data to new pages while preserving the committed page map.
answer.explanation: ADB29 preserves the committed version and writes changed data at new locations. Shadow paging keeps the old page map plus a modified map; commit atomically installs the new durable root after needed pages are durable. B captures the copy-on-write preservation, although the unchanged old map is the shadow rather than the name of each newly modified page.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A separate-server backup is not the page-map copy-on-write mechanism of shadow paging.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Changes use new pages, preserving the originals until the new committed map is safely installed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Encryption does not preserve the old page mapping or provide the stated rollback mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sorting pages is an access-layout choice rather than preserving committed copies.

evidence.quote: In-place update overwrites the original location. Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version. Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable. Before commit, a crash uses the old map. It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.
A full backup copies the database to separate storage; scheduled backups plus archived logs support restoration to a chosen recoverable point.
Rollback handles failed/uncommitted work; redo preserves committed work missing from pages; checkpoints reduce log-search work; backups provide another stored copy.

questions.stem: Which type of database failure is caused by accidental deletion of important data by a user?
questions.hint: Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 42

answer.text: Human error.
answer.explanation: The described cause is an accidental user action, not faulty hardware, a natural event or a software defect. ADB26 treats human mistakes separately and notes they may need point-in-time restoration before a bad committed operation. Ordinary crash redo would otherwise preserve a committed deletion rather than recognize the user’s intention.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: No hardware malfunction is stated; the cause is the user's mistaken deletion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A natural disaster is not the cause described in the prompt.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The software may have executed the requested deletion correctly; the stated mistake belongs to the user.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Accidental deletion by a user is a human error.

evidence.quote: Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts. Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure. A system crash loses volatile memory while disks may survive. Media failure damages persistent storage and normally requires restoring a backup, then replaying available archived logs. Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation.
An accidental user deletion is human error even if the software executes the requested command correctly.
A software failure originates in erroneous program behavior, such as a logical programming defect, invalid operation or operating-system fault.

questions.stem: The transaction log records 'before and after values' for data modifications primarily to support:

options.label: C
options.text: UNDO (restore old value) and REDO (apply new value) operations during recovery

questions.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 43

answer.text: Undo with old values and redo with logged new values.
answer.explanation: ADB27 restores before-images when undoing incomplete work and installs after-images when redoing logged effects. Recording both values therefore supports reversal and reapplication after failure. Query costing uses catalog statistics, access control uses privileges, and compression is a different storage concern; none explains the specific recovery value pair as directly.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Query optimization estimates plan cost rather than restoring old/new transaction values.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Access control checks privileges rather than using before/after images to authorize users.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Old values support reversal and new values support necessary reapplication during recovery.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Recording two values can add storage overhead and is not primarily a compression mechanism.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.
A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic.
Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions.

questions.stem: Which type of distributed database uses the SAME DBMS software at every site?
questions.hint: Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 44

answer.text: Homogeneous distributed database.
answer.explanation: ADB33 identifies homogeneous systems by compatible DBMS technology across sites. Using the same DBMS software fits that classification. Heterogeneous systems integrate differing engines, models or interfaces. Middleware describes integration architecture and partial replication describes placement of copies, so neither substitutes for the homogeneity classification asked for here.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Heterogeneous systems integrate differing database technologies rather than the same DBMS throughout.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Using the same DBMS at each site fits homogeneous distributed database technology.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Middleware describes communication/integration responsibilities, not whether DBMS technology is the same.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Partial replication describes where selected copies reside rather than which DBMS software sites use.

evidence.quote: A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system. A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces. Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction. Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization.
Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.
These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.

questions.stem: Horizontal fragmentation divides a table based on:

options.label: B
options.text: Splitting rows into subsets based on a condition

options.label: C
options.text: Combining two tables into one larger table

options.label: D
options.text: Replicating the table to multiple sites

questions.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 45

answer.text: Split rows by predicates.
answer.explanation: ADB36 defines horizontal fragmentation as selecting row subsets using predicates and reconstructing the relation by union. Column subsets belong to vertical fragmentation. Combining tables is not fragmentation, and copying a whole table is replication. Thus B identifies both the item being split and the rule used to decide fragment membership.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Column splitting is vertical fragmentation rather than horizontal fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Horizontal fragments contain rows selected by stated predicates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Combining tables increases the combined relation rather than splitting one table into row subsets.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replicating copies preserves the whole table at more sites rather than partitioning its rows.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.
Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.

questions.stem: In vertical fragmentation, why must the PRIMARY KEY be included in every fragment?

options.label: C
options.text: To enable reconstruction of the original table by joining fragments on the primary key

options.label: D
options.text: To ensure proper replication across sites

questions.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 46

answer.text: A repeated key or row identifier lets vertical pieces join back losslessly.
answer.explanation: ADB36 repeats a key or row identifier across vertical fragments so attributes from the same original row can be matched during reconstruction. C states that purpose. The general requirement is a suitable identifier, not necessarily the particular declared primary key if another row identifier is used. It is unrelated to mandatory replication or inherently faster inserts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Faster insertion is not why vertical fragments share a row identifier.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Avoiding duplicate values is not sufficient to align column pieces from the same original row.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The shared key identifies matching original rows when the column fragments are joined.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replication copies data and is distinct from reconstructing vertical column fragments.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.
Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.

questions.stem: Which data replication scheme stores each data fragment at ONLY ONE site with NO copies?
questions.hint: Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 47

answer.text: No replication, or nonredundant allocation.
answer.explanation: ADB37 explicitly calls storing each fragment once nonredundant allocation. Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site, while partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites. A hybrid can mix strategies, but the stem specifies exactly one location and no copies for every fragment, so C is the precise classification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Full replication stores copies throughout the relevant sites rather than one copy per fragment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Partial replication still copies selected fragments and therefore does not mean no copies.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nonredundant allocation stores each fragment at one site without replicas.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A hybrid can combine policies, but the stated universal no-copy arrangement is specifically nonreplicated.

evidence.quote: Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.
Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.
Snapshot replication transfers a copy at intervals; incremental replication transfers changes.

questions.stem: Transparency in distributed databases means that:

options.label: A
options.text: All data is encrypted and transparent to hackers

options.label: B
options.text: The distribution complexity is hidden from users who interact as if using a single database

options.label: C
options.text: Users can see all technical details of how data is distributed

options.label: D
options.text: All sites must use the same operating system

questions.hint: Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 48

answer.text: Hide distribution details behind a single logical database experience.
answer.explanation: ADB35 defines transparency through which distribution details are hidden: sites, fragment reconstruction or replica selection/maintenance. Together these can let clients work with a single logical database abstraction. B captures that broad meaning. Transparency is not encryption, disclosure of every technical detail or a requirement that operating systems be identical.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encryption protects content; transparency here concerns hiding distribution complexity from legitimate users.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Distribution details can be hidden so users work with one logical database abstraction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transparency hides selected implementation details rather than exposing all of them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Operating-system uniformity does not define distribution transparency.

evidence.quote: Location transparency hides which site holds a named object. Fragmentation transparency hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments: users query the whole logical relation. Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained. The broad single-logical-database experience may involve all three.
Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction.
Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions.

questions.stem: Hybrid fragmentation combines which two fragmentation types?
questions.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 49

answer.text: Horizontal and vertical fragmentation.
answer.explanation: ADB36 defines hybrid fragmentation as combining row and column splits in a suitable order. Reconstructing reverses those operations using unions for horizontal pieces and key joins for corresponding vertical pieces. Replication, deployment architectures and DBMS homogeneity are different design dimensions rather than the two fragmentation types combined by hybrid fragmentation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replication copies data and is not the second fragmentation dimension in the hybrid definition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hybrid fragmentation combines horizontal row splits with vertical column splits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Client-server and middleware classify architectures rather than fragmentation operations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Homogeneous/heterogeneous classifies system technology compatibility rather than row/column splitting.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.
Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.

questions.stem: With full replication and synchronous propagation before acknowledgment, which listed disadvantage specifically concerns maintaining copies during an update-heavy workload? Assume usable replicas can serve reads.

options.label: A
options.text: Data becomes unavailable when any site fails

options.label: B
options.text: Updates incur propagation and coordination overhead because changes must reach the required copies before acknowledgment.

options.label: C
options.text: It requires all sites to use the same DBMS software

options.label: D
options.text: Queries can only be answered from the primary site

questions.hint: Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 50

answer.text: B. Updates incur propagation and coordination overhead because changes must reach the required copies before acknowledgment.
answer.explanation: Full replication stores the entire database at each relevant site, so updates create propagation and coordination work. The stated synchronous policy places that work before acknowledgment, adding update latency in the update-heavy scenario. This is the disadvantage described by B. Usable copies can serve reads and improve availability; full replication neither implies identical DBMS software nor restricts queries to one primary site.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usable replicas can keep data available after one site fails.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stated synchronous policy adds propagation and coordination work before acknowledgment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Full replication is a copy-placement policy, not a requirement to standardize every DBMS.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Usable replicas can serve reads in the stated scenario.

evidence.quote: Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.
Eager/synchronous replication coordinates propagation before the specified commit/acknowledgment point, increasing update latency.
Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.

questions.stem: What does ACID stand for in database transactions?
questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 1

answer.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
answer.explanation: ADB06 gives all-or-none effects, preservation of declared rules, controlled interference and persistence after failure as the four ACID properties. B names them correctly. The other options substitute concurrency, availability, integrity, correctness or distribution for the defined terms, changing the acronym rather than describing an equivalent expansion.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Concurrency incorrectly replaces Consistency in the acronym.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The expansion exactly matches the four ACID property names.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Availability and Integrity replace Atomicity and Isolation, which are the defined terms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Correctness and Distribution do not replace Consistency and Durability in ACID.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.

questions.stem: Which ACID property ensures that either ALL operations of a transaction complete or NONE do?
questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 2

answer.text: Atomicity.
answer.explanation: The requested property concerns whether partial transaction effects can survive. ADB06 assigns all-or-none application to atomicity. A correct transaction also preserves consistency, concurrency needs isolation and completed commits need durability, but those are different guarantees. C is therefore the property matching the explicit ALL or NONE condition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns preservation of integrity rules rather than the indivisible effect boundary itself.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Isolation governs concurrent interference rather than all-or-none transaction effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Atomicity makes the transaction effects succeed together or be removed together.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Durability protects committed effects rather than defining partial-success handling.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.

questions.stem: If A=5000 and B=8000, and 750 is transferred from A to B, what values satisfy the Consistency property?
questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 3

answer.explanation: Subtracting 750 from A gives 4250 and adding it to B gives 8750; their total remains 13000. A implements both the specified operation and its total-balance invariant. B and C apply only one side. D preserves the initial total but does not perform the requested transfer, so invariant preservation alone does not make it the successful-transfer result.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It performs the 750 debit and credit and preserves the total of 13000.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The debit occurs without its credit, reducing the total to 12250.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The credit occurs without its debit, increasing the total to 13750.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It preserves the starting total but leaves both accounts unchanged rather than performing the transfer.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.
Unchanged or reverse-transfer balances can also preserve that sum; only the requested debit/credit implements the specified successful transfer.
Both balances total 13,000.

questions.stem: Which ACID property ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other?
questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 4

answer.text: Isolation.
answer.explanation: ADB06 assigns concurrent-interference control to isolation. That is the distinguishing phrase in the stem. Atomicity handles partial effects, durability handles committed persistence, and consistency means correct work preserves declared rules. Different isolation levels provide different detailed guarantees, so this classification does not imply that all implementations offer serializability by default.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Atomicity governs partial effects within a transaction rather than concurrent interference.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Durability concerns persistence of committed changes after failures.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns declared integrity rules under correct business logic.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Isolation controls interference among concurrently executing transactions.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.

questions.stem: Which ACID property guarantees committed changes survive system crashes?
questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 5

answer.text: Durability.
answer.explanation: ADB06 defines durability by persistence of committed effects despite failure. Recovery information can provide this even when changed data pages were buffered at the instant of commit. All-or-none application, invariant preservation and concurrent isolation serve different transaction guarantees, so only durability matches survival of successful commits after a crash.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Atomicity concerns all-or-none application rather than the persistence of completed commits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns validity of declared invariants rather than crash survival of commits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Isolation controls concurrent interactions rather than persistence after a crash.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Durability preserves committed effects across system failures.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.

questions.stem: A transaction that has executed all operations but NOT YET committed is in which state?
questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 6

answer.text: Partially committed.
answer.explanation: ADB06 places a transaction in Partially committed after its last operation finishes but before durable commitment is assured. The stem states exactly that boundary. Active means operations are still executing; Committed needs successful commit; Failed needs an error. Finishing the operation list alone does not establish the committed state.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Active describes ongoing operation execution, not the interval after the last operation finishes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The last operation finished, but commitment is not yet assured.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The stem explicitly says the transaction has not yet committed.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No execution or commit failure is reported.

evidence.quote: Active means operations are executing. Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured. Committed means commitment succeeded. A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt. Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation; recovery supports atomicity and durability. Transaction management is the broader subsystem, so both it and recovery management can be legitimate answers to broad responsibility questions.

questions.stem: In the Aborted state, what happens to all changes made by the transaction?

options.label: B
options.text: All changes are rolled back restoring the database to its pre-transaction state

questions.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
