sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 7

answer.text: Its effects have been rolled back; other committed transactions remain.
answer.explanation: ADB06 reaches Aborted after rollback. Thus the aborted transaction’s own changes are removed rather than permanently saved. Restoring pre-transaction state must be understood relative to its effects, not erasing unrelated concurrent commits. A restart can be a new attempt, but is not automatic merely because the aborted state was reached.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Permanent saving is a committed outcome, not an aborted outcome.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rollback removes this transaction's effects while retaining other transactions' legitimate committed work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waiting for a lock describes a blocked executing transaction rather than completed rollback.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An aborted transaction may be retried, but automatic restart is not guaranteed.

evidence.quote: Active means operations are executing. Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured. Committed means commitment succeeded. A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt. Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation; recovery supports atomicity and durability. Transaction management is the broader subsystem, so both it and recovery management can be legitimate answers to broad responsibility questions.
Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward.
Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk.

questions.stem: Which log record signals successful completion of transaction T?
questions.hint: Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 8

answer.text: [commit, T].
answer.explanation: ADB07 identifies COMMIT as the record of successful transaction completion. START begins work, UPDATE records a data change and ABORT marks failed termination/rollback handling. A data write by itself does not prove the enclosing transaction committed, and an abort record can begin rollback rather than confirm it has completed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The start record indicates beginning work rather than successful completion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Abort records failure/rollback handling instead of successful commitment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An update record describes one changed item, not successful transaction completion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The commit record signals successful completion of transaction T.

evidence.quote: A conceptual log can contain START, UPDATE(T,X,old,new), COMMIT, ABORT and END records. Before-images support undo; after-images support redo. Real systems may use physical or logical records, and need not log every read. COMMIT records successful completion; an ABORT record can mark the start of rollback rather than prove every undo step is complete.

questions.stem: The Read_item(X) command transfers data in which order?
questions.hint: Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 9

answer.text: Disk page → buffer → program variable.
answer.explanation: ADB07 locates X’s page, loads it into a buffer if absent and copies the item from that buffer into the program variable. C gives that conceptual data movement order. A cached page may avoid the physical disk read, but the program still reads through the buffer. The reverse direction describes a write path rather than read_item.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The page is buffered before the item is copied to the program variable.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A read does not first send the buffer to disk before obtaining the variable value.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The page enters the buffer if needed, then its item is copied into the program variable.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Program-variable-to-buffer-to-disk describes writing, not reading into a variable.

evidence.quote: read_item(X) locates X's page, brings it into a buffer if absent, and copies X into a program variable. write_item(X) copies the new program value into the buffered page, marking it dirty. Writing that page to disk can occur later according to the buffer policy; write_item is not inherently an immediate disk flush. Insert and delete also modify data; sorting is a query-processing operation rather than a primitive item update.
Real systems may use physical or logical records, and need not log every read.
Before-images support undo; after-images support redo.

questions.stem: In a multi-user system, which mechanisms does the DBMS use to manage concurrent access?
questions.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 10

answer.text: Locks, timestamp rules and transaction scheduling.
answer.explanation: ADB11 defines compatible shared/exclusive locks and ADB15 orders conflicting operations with timestamp tests. These are actual concurrency-control mechanisms that constrain transaction schedules. Backups provide copies for recovery, and file permissions determine access rather than safe interleavings. Physical separation of people also does not coordinate their concurrent database operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Backups support restoration rather than scheduling safe concurrent reads and writes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Locks and timestamp rules control conflicting accesses and permissible schedules.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Separating users physically does not coordinate their concurrent operations on shared database items.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: File permissions alone do not enforce isolation among authorized concurrent transactions.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts.
Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes.

questions.stem: The Lost Update problem is also called:
questions.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 11

answer.text: Write-write problem, as shorthand for a lost-update overwrite.
answer.explanation: ADB08 illustrates both transactions reading 500, one writing 700 and the other later overwriting it with stale 600. The conflict is between their writes, which explains the offered write-write shorthand. This is not a claim that every pair of writes loses an update: the stale calculation and overwrite are essential. Read/read and phantom behavior describe different situations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two reads alone do not overwrite and lose an update.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stale write overwrites another write, motivating this write-write shorthand.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The defining loss is the later stale overwrite, not merely an arbitrary read/write pair.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A phantom changes a predicate query's qualifying row set rather than overwriting one balance.

evidence.quote: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.

questions.stem: A Dirty Read occurs when:

options.label: A
options.text: A transaction reads only committed data

options.label: B
options.text: A transaction reads data modified by another uncommitted transaction

options.label: C
options.text: Two transactions read the same record simultaneously

options.label: D
options.text: A transaction writes invalid format data

questions.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 12

answer.text: Reading another transaction’s uncommitted data.
answer.explanation: ADB08 defines dirty read through another transaction’s uncommitted write. The value can disappear if its writer aborts, leaving dependent work based on invalid data. Reading committed data or two readers accessing one item is not inherently dirty. Invalid-format writes concern data validity rather than whether the read-from transaction has committed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reading only committed values avoids the defining uncommitted-writer dependency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The read consumes another transaction's modification before that writer commits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple readers alone do not create an uncommitted data dependency.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Invalid format concerns validation or integrity rather than the definition of a dirty read.

evidence.quote: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.

questions.stem: Which trace demonstrates an incorrect-summary anomaly, meaning an aggregate that mixes mutually inconsistent versions? Treat nonrepeatable read as a separate anomaly.

options.label: A
options.text: A transaction reads data after another commits

options.label: B
options.text: Initially A=B=100. T2 transfers 10 from A to B while T1 reads old A=100 and new B=110, reporting 210 rather than the invariant total 200.

options.label: C
options.text: Two transactions delete the same record

options.label: D
options.text: A transaction reads its own uncommitted data

questions.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 13

answer.text: B. Initially A=B=100. T2 transfers 10 from A to B while T1 reads old A=100 and new B=110, reporting 210 rather than the invariant total 200.
answer.explanation: The transfer subtracts and adds the same amount, preserving a total of 200. T1 instead adds an old A balance to a new B balance and obtains 210, combining versions that do not form a consistent summary. That is the incorrect-summary anomaly. Reading committed data, deleting a record or reading one's own uncommitted changes alone does not establish this aggregate defect.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A read after another commit is not by itself an inconsistent aggregate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 100+110=210 mixes versions and violates the preserved total 200.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent deletions alone do not show this summary anomaly.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reading one's own changes is not the stated mixed-version aggregate.

evidence.quote: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.
Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200.
A single committed update from B=20 to B=50 does not alone prove an invalid summary of 90.

questions.stem: A Shared Lock allows:

options.label: A
options.text: Only one transaction to read an item

options.label: B
options.text: Multiple transactions to read simultaneously but not write

options.label: C
options.text: One transaction to read and write exclusively

questions.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 14

answer.text: Compatible readers, with no writing under a shared lock.
answer.explanation: ADB11 permits multiple shared locks on one item, each for reading. Writing requires a suitable exclusive lock, which conflicts with other shared holders. Thus B describes shared-lock behavior in the basic lock-based model. Exclusive read/write ownership and multiple simultaneous writers are not shared locking; multiversion snapshot rules are a separate model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: More than one transaction may hold compatible shared read locks on the same item.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared locks permit multiple readers but do not authorize writes under that lock mode.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sole read/write ownership describes an exclusive lock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shared locks do not allow multiple transactions to write simultaneously.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.
No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

questions.stem: An Exclusive Lock allows:

options.label: C
options.text: Only one transaction to both read and write, blocking all other access

options.label: D
options.text: Multiple readers and one writer simultaneously

questions.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 15

answer.text: The exclusive holder may read and write; conflicting access to that item is blocked.
answer.explanation: ADB11 permits an exclusive lock holder to read and write and makes that item’s X lock conflict with another S or X. C is correct in this basic model. Blocking all other access means conflicting access to the same item, not the entire database; locks on other items remain independent and multiversion systems can have additional snapshot-reader behavior.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Other transactions' shared reads conflict with an exclusive lock on the same item in this model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Two exclusive writers cannot hold compatible locks on the same item.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One holder can read/write the locked item while incompatible same-item accesses wait or abort.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Concurrent same-item shared readers conflict with this exclusive writer under the basic rules.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.
S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave.

questions.stem: In Two-Phase Locking (2PL), during the Growing Phase a transaction:
questions.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 16

answer.text: Acquire or upgrade locks without releasing them.
answer.explanation: ADB12 defines growing as the acquisition/upgrade phase and shrinking as the release/downgrade phase. Once any lock is released, no further acquisition is allowed. B therefore matches growing. Freely mixing acquisition and release would abandon the two-phase discipline that guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Releasing locks belongs to shrinking rather than growing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Growing acquires or upgrades locks before any release occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Freely acquiring after release violates the defining 2PL phase restriction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Growing is precisely the phase in which lock requests may be made.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.

questions.stem: Which concurrency control technique uses start-times to order transaction execution?
questions.hint: Compare the transaction timestamp with the item's recorded read and write timestamps.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 17

answer.text: Timestamp-based concurrency control.
answer.explanation: ADB15 assigns each transaction a timestamp and checks reads and writes against item read/write timestamps. These checks preserve timestamp order and can abort stale operations. Locking instead uses ownership compatibility, optimistic control validates private work and shadow paging concerns recovery page maps. Only C names the start-time ordering technique described.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locking uses lock compatibility and protocols rather than being defined by transaction start-time ordering.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimistic control validates private read/write sets rather than applying these timestamp-order tests.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Timestamp-based control orders valid conflicting operations using transaction timestamps.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves committed page maps for recovery rather than ordering concurrent operations.

evidence.quote: Assign each transaction TS(T). For item X track read_TS(X), the largest timestamp of a successful reader, and write_TS(X), that of its latest successful writer. A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS. A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS. These tests preserve timestamp order.
Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.

questions.stem: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is best suited for:

options.label: B
options.text: Read-heavy workloads where conflicts are rare

questions.hint: Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 18

answer.text: Read-heavy, low-conflict workloads.
answer.explanation: ADB16 computes privately, validates and publishes, retrying failed validation. Low-conflict workloads let most work succeed; high write contention wastes computation on aborts. B states that criterion explicitly. Single-user systems do not need intertransaction conflict control, and OCC is not restricted to distributed transactions. Actual conflict frequency matters more than the read-heavy label alone.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: High conflicts cause validation failures and repeated wasted work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rare conflicts allow optimistic private work to validate successfully with few retries.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A single-user setting lacks the concurrent conflict problem motivating this choice.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Optimistic control is not limited to distributed transaction environments.

evidence.quote: Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries. It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts. Multiversion control keeps versions so a reader can use an appropriate snapshot. Snapshot isolation is not automatically serializable: concurrent writes to different rows can violate a shared invariant.

questions.stem: Deadlock occurs when:

options.label: A
options.text: One transaction waits for a resource held by no one

options.label: B
options.text: Two or more transactions each wait for resources held by the other in a circular chain

questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 19

answer.text: A circular resource-wait chain.
answer.explanation: ADB13 requires a waiting cycle: participants hold resources needed by others and cannot make progress without a victim release or another intervention. Waiting for an unheld resource does not state such a cycle. Slow commit and simultaneous reads can occur without deadlock; compatible shared readers in particular need not block one another.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A resource held by no one does not create the stated circular hold-and-wait dependency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Each participant waits for another holder in a cycle, preventing independent progress.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A slow commit may still progress and need not form a waiting cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compatible shared reads of the same data do not inherently deadlock.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.
No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

questions.stem: In the Wait-Die protocol, when a YOUNGER transaction requests a resource held by an OLDER transaction:
questions.hint: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 20

answer.text: The younger requester aborts.
answer.explanation: The requester is younger and the holder older. ADB14 makes that requester die in wait–die; only an older requester may wait for a younger holder. On retry the aborted transaction retains its original timestamp. Wounding a holder belongs to a different protocol, and both participants need not be aborted.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Wait–die aborts the younger requester when the needed resource is held by an older transaction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The older holder keeps its resource; this protocol does not kill it for a younger requester.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waiting is allowed for an older requester facing a younger holder, not this case.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The policy aborts the younger requester, not both participants.

evidence.quote: A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.
Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive.
In wait–die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one; a younger transaction requesting a resource held by an older one aborts.

questions.stem: In the Wound-Wait protocol, when an OLDER transaction requests a resource held by a YOUNGER transaction:

options.label: B
options.text: The younger is wounded (aborted), allowing the older to proceed

questions.hint: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 21

answer.text: Abort the younger holder so the older requester can proceed.
answer.explanation: ADB14 says an older requester wounds a younger holder, while a younger requester waits. B is therefore the rule for the given ages. The protocol uses priority to prevent cycles rather than arbitrarily aborting both or handing the work to a new transaction. Any retry should preserve the original timestamp to reduce starvation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under this policy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The younger holder is aborted, releasing the resource for the older requester.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Aborting both is unnecessary and is not the wound–wait rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No replacement transaction takes over; the older requester continues after the conflicting holder releases.

evidence.quote: A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.
Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive.
In wait–die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one; a younger transaction requesting a resource held by an older one aborts.

questions.stem: Lock Timeout as a deadlock solution works by:

options.label: B
options.text: Aborting any transaction that waits longer than a specified time limit

options.label: C
options.text: Locking all items before a transaction starts

questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 22

answer.text: Abort a transaction whose wait exceeds the configured limit.
answer.explanation: ADB13 defines timeout by excessive wait duration and warns it can mistake slow progress for deadlock. B matches that mechanism. Wait-for graphs detect cycles, conservative locking obtains all locks before execution and age priorities define wait–die/wound–wait decisions. Those are distinct policies rather than implementations of a time limit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Graph analysis detects cycles rather than deciding from elapsed lock-wait time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Timeout aborts a waiting transaction after its configured wait limit is exceeded.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Preacquiring all locks is conservative locking rather than timeout handling.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Age-based priorities define other prevention policies, not an elapsed-wait threshold.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.
Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.

questions.stem: A schedule is serializable if:

options.label: A
options.text: All transactions execute one after another with no overlap

options.label: B
options.text: Its concurrent execution produces the same result as some serial execution of those transactions

options.label: C
options.text: All transactions commit at the same time

options.label: D
options.text: No two transactions access the same table

questions.hint: Distinguish transaction ordering, conflict conditions and full execution equivalence.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 23

answer.text: Equivalent behavior to some serial execution, even if interleaved.
answer.explanation: ADB09 defines a serializable schedule as equivalent to a serial order while permitting interleaving. B matches when same result means the required full transaction equivalence, not an accidental equality of one final value. A describes a serial schedule, which is a special case but not the general definition. Commit simultaneity and disjoint tables are not required.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This defines serial execution, a stricter special case that omits permitted serializable interleavings.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Serializable behavior is equivalent to some serial ordering; coincidental equality of one value alone is insufficient.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Simultaneous commits do not establish the required transaction-execution equivalence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Serializable transactions may access the same tables if their operations are correctly ordered.

evidence.quote: A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions. Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read/read pairs do not conflict.

questions.stem: Lock Upgrade refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: Releasing an exclusive lock to a shared lock

options.label: B
options.text: Converting a shared (read) lock to an exclusive (write) lock

options.label: D
options.text: Granting a lock to multiple transactions

questions.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 24

answer.text: Convert Shared to Exclusive.
answer.explanation: ADB11 identifies S→X as an upgrade, possible only after incompatible other holders leave. It strengthens an existing read lock to permit writing. X→S is a downgrade, releasing all locks is transaction cleanup and granting compatible readers is shared acquisition. Only B names the requested conversion of a held lock.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-shared is a downgrade rather than an upgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the lock to permit writing when compatibility allows.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Removing locks is release rather than conversion to a stronger mode.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Granting compatible shared readers is not the upgrade of one existing lock.

evidence.quote: A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks. S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave. X→S is a downgrade. The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests. One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy. No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

questions.stem: Starvation in concurrency control means:

options.label: A
options.text: A transaction holding too many locks

options.label: B
options.text: A transaction is perpetually delayed and never executes due to other transactions always taking priority

options.label: C
options.text: The database runs out of storage space

options.label: D
options.text: A transaction commits before completing all operations

questions.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 25

answer.text: Indefinite postponement caused by repeated priority to other work.
answer.explanation: ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other transactions progress, without requiring a deadlock cycle. B states that repeated bypass precisely. Holding many locks can create contention but does not itself prove starvation. Storage exhaustion and premature commit are different failures, so neither supplies the scheduling-fairness definition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Holding many locks describes resource use rather than being perpetually denied execution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated priority to others can indefinitely postpone the transaction while other work continues.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Running out of storage is a capacity failure rather than the defined scheduling starvation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Premature commit concerns transaction correctness rather than indefinite postponement.

evidence.quote: Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.

questions.stem: The first step in SQL query processing is:
questions.hint: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 26

answer.text: Parsing and translation.
answer.explanation: ADB17 first checks syntax and semantics and constructs a logical query representation, before optimization and evaluation. C groups those initial activities. Result delivery follows execution, while optimization needs an understood query to compare valid plans. The phase grouping is conventional, but the ordering dependency is explicit in the complete note.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Optimization follows understanding and representing the query rather than preceding it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Evaluation executes a selected plan and is not the first processing activity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Parsing/translation establishes query meaning and logical representation before optimization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Results can be delivered only after the required evaluation produces them.

evidence.quote: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.
Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.
DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence.

questions.stem: SQL queries are internally translated into:
questions.hint: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 27

answer.text: Relational algebra.
answer.explanation: ADB17 translates a query into relational algebra or a logical query tree for equivalent rewrites and plan selection. B names that logical representation. A particular engine may later compile execution code, but machine code, Python scripts and XML documents are not the general logical translation target taught here. Logical meaning precedes implementation-specific execution choices.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Machine code may be an implementation detail but is not the stated logical translation target.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Relational algebra represents the logical operations used for rewriting and planning.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Python scripts are not the general internal representation specified here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: XML documents are not the defined general relational query representation.

evidence.quote: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.
A physical execution plan adds scan/index choices and algorithms.
A query tree has base relations at leaves and operators at internal nodes; a query graph emphasizes relations and predicates.

questions.stem: What does query optimization aim to minimize?

options.label: B
options.text: The overall cost (time and resources) of executing the query

options.label: D
options.text: The character length of the SQL query

questions.hint: Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 28

answer.text: Overall execution cost under the chosen resource model.
answer.explanation: ADB19 measures candidate plans using I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. The aim is a suitable low-cost equivalent plan, not syntactic brevity or indiscriminate removal of joins and tables. Required tables and semantics must be preserved; even fewer operations do not necessarily imply lower runtime or resource cost.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Required tables cannot be discarded merely to reduce the table count.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimization compares equivalent plans using estimated time and resource costs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Join count alone ignores access paths, cardinalities and the cost of each join.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Short SQL text does not necessarily produce a cheaper execution plan.

evidence.quote: A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions. Selection with fraction s predicts s×N rows. For non-NULL equijoin keys, a common estimate is |R|×|S|/max(V(R,k),V(S,k)), assuming uniform values and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain within the larger. Adjust counts for NULLs; if either non-NULL input is empty, the result is zero. Skew, correlations or incomplete domain overlap can invalidate this estimate; known disjoint domains give zero matches.
Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans.
For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time.

questions.stem: Database recovery restores the database after failure to:

options.label: B
options.text: A consistent and correct state, undoing incomplete transactions and reapplying committed ones

options.label: C
options.text: The state at the last user login

options.label: D
options.text: An empty state for fresh start

sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 31

answer.text: A valid recovered state preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.
answer.explanation: ADB26 defines restart recovery by preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects after failure. B matches the simple undo/redo teaching model. The detailed work depends on buffer policy and algorithm; not every committed update needs physical redo if already installed. Recovery does not reset the database to creation, last login or an empty replacement state.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Returning to creation would discard legitimate later durable commits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Recovery preserves committed work and removes incomplete effects to restore valid state.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: User login time is not the transaction recovery boundary.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Emptying the database would destroy committed data rather than recover it.

evidence.quote: Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts. Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure. A system crash loses volatile memory while disks may survive. Media failure damages persistent storage and normally requires restoring a backup, then replaying available archived logs. Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation.

answer.text: Software error.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The stated cause is faulty software behavior rather than a malfunctioning hardware component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No natural event is described; the prompt names a software bug.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Unexpected behavior caused by DBMS bugs is a software error.

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: A software failure originates in erroneous program behavior, such as a logical programming defect, invalid operation or operating-system fault. questions.stem: What does WAL require? In B, 'corresponding data changes' specifically means durable output of the changed data page; volatile buffer changes may occur earlier.

options.label: A

options.label: B

answer.text: B. Log records written to stable storage BEFORE corresponding data changes
answer.explanation: The update log needed for recovery must be stable before the changed data page becomes persistent. B states that order under the question's explicit durable-write meaning. The buffer can be modified earlier. Data-before-log reverses the rule, waiting until after commit is not the required logging policy and checkpointing before every write is not a WAL requirement.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk. To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage. A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.
Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not.

answer.text: C. REDO only; D. NO UNDO / REDO
answer.explanation: Because uncommitted changes have not reached the persistent database, crash recovery does not need to undo them there. Undo-only and undo/redo both assert an undo requirement that this deferred model avoids.

choices.label: D

answer.text: C. Both old (before-image) AND new (after-image) values

answer.text: Logically related data across networked sites under coordinated database management.
answer.explanation: ADB33 defines logically related data across networked sites managed as a coordinated system. B matches that architecture and its logical abstraction. options.label: D
options.text: Fragments are listed as separate tables in the schema

questions.hint: Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 48

answer.text: Users query the logical relation without knowing its fragments.
answer.explanation: ADB35 defines fragmentation transparency as hiding the existence and reconstruction of fragments. B states that user-facing abstraction directly. It does not require literally only DBAs to know the implementation; developers and administrators may also need that knowledge. Exposing fragment tables or all fragmentation details to users would make fragmentation visible instead of transparent.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Showing all fragmentation details is the opposite of hiding them from ordinary queries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Users operate on the whole logical relation without managing its fragment reconstruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transparency describes the user abstraction, not exclusive knowledge restricted to DBAs alone.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Naming fragments separately exposes fragmentation rather than concealing it from the querying user.

evidence.quote: Location transparency hides which site holds a named object. Fragmentation transparency hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments: users query the whole logical relation. Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained. The broad single-logical-database experience may involve all three.
If users explicitly name a fragment but need not specify its site, fragmentation is visible while location can remain transparent.
Hiding this column split from queries is fragmentation transparency; the split itself is a data-design operation.

questions.stem: The Middleware architecture in distributed DBMS uses:

options.label: B
options.text: All servers collaborating on every query

options.label: C
options.text: A dedicated middleware server that mediates between clients and multiple independent database servers

questions.hint: Identify which tier submits, mediates or executes a request.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 49

answer.text: Middleware mediates between clients and independent database servers.
answer.explanation: ADB34 lets middleware translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. C describes that mediating tier. The logical responsibility does not require exactly one physical machine in every implementation. Direct connections omit this mediator, universal server collaboration is a different arrangement, and one centralized server is not the stated distributed middleware design.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Direct client-server links alone omit the middleware mediation that defines the requested architecture.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every server need not participate in every query; relevant sources depend on the request.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A middleware tier mediates client requests across multiple independent database servers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One centralized database server does not describe mediation across independent distributed servers.

evidence.quote: In client/server architecture, clients submit requests while servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules. In collaborating-server designs, servers cooperate on subqueries and transactions. Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.

questions.stem: Hybrid fragmentation combines which two techniques?
questions.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
sources: Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 50

answer.text: Horizontal and vertical fragmentation.
answer.explanation: ADB36 explicitly defines hybrid fragmentation as combining row and column splits in an appropriate order. B names those two operations. Replication changes copy placement, locking and timestamps control concurrent access, and client-server/middleware describe architecture responsibilities. They can coexist with hybrid fragmentation but are not its two component fragmentation techniques.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Full/no replication concerns copies rather than the row and column splits of hybrid fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hybrid fragmentation combines horizontal row subsets with vertical column subsets.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Locking and timestamps are concurrency-control mechanisms, not fragmentation types.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: These are architecture forms rather than the two data-fragmentation operations.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.
These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.

questions.stem: In client-server database architecture, what is the primary role of the server?

options.label: A
options.text: Provide the GUI for end users

options.label: B
options.text: Initiate all network connections and poll clients for updates

options.label: C
options.text: Store and manage shared data, enforce ACID properties, and process client requests

options.label: D
options.text: Cache all user sessions locally for offline access

questions.hint: Identify which tier submits, mediates or executes a request.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 3

answer.text: Manage shared data, process requests and enforce supported transaction/integrity guarantees.
answer.explanation: ADB34 assigns clients request submission and servers shared-data management, operation execution and supported integrity/transaction enforcement. C matches those responsibilities. User interfaces usually belong to clients, while initiating all connections, polling every client or caching all sessions for offline use are not the server role defined by this architecture. Guarantees still depend on supported mechanisms and correct application use.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The user-facing GUI is normally a client responsibility rather than the database server's primary role.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The server need not initiate every connection or poll clients for every update.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared-data management, query execution and supported integrity/transaction enforcement are server duties.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Caching every session for offline access is not the defined database-server responsibility.

evidence.quote: In client/server architecture, clients submit requests while servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules. In collaborating-server designs, servers cooperate on subqueries and transactions. Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.
Calling a system heterogeneous does not require all sites to surrender autonomy or to copy every row everywhere.
A tightly integrated distributed system can present one global schema and shared control.

questions.stem:
In two-phase locking (2PL), during which phase may a transaction acquire locks but not 
release any?
questions.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 5

answer.text: Growing phase.
answer.explanation: ADB12 allows acquiring or upgrading locks during growing and releasing or downgrading them during shrinking. Once any lock is released, a transaction may not acquire another. A is therefore the phase described. Commit is a transaction event, validation belongs to optimistic control and shrinking has the opposite lock-release role.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Growing permits acquisitions and upgrades before any release starts.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Commit is not the general 2PL phase for new lock acquisition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Validation is an optimistic-control stage rather than the 2PL growing phase.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shrinking releases or downgrades locks and forbids acquiring new ones.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.

questions.stem:
Assume that we are able to specify that Mr. Getahun can view the database record, but 
cannot change the value of the record. Which security management technique was used in 
this scenario?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario concerns identity, permission, disclosure or valid values.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 27

answer.text: Access control.
answer.explanation: ADB24 explicitly describes a user allowed to view but not change a record as having restricted access privileges. That is authorization/access control. Integrity concerns valid values, availability concerns readiness for use and non-repudiation concerns attributable actions rather than whether a particular read or write is permitted. A matches the actual permission distinction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Access control grants reading while denying modification for the specified user.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Availability concerns service readiness rather than the read-versus-write privilege distinction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Non-repudiation does not define whether this user is authorized to modify a record.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Integrity restricts valid data states rather than assigning user-specific read/update permissions.

evidence.quote: Authentication establishes identity; authorization/access control determines permitted actions. Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions. A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges. A view can restrict visible rows/columns, but its privilege and execution rules must support that restriction.
Neither property specifies which particular user has permission to change a database row; that is the separate authorization decision.
Availability concerns keeping services and resources accessible to their authorized users.

questions.stem:
Suppose, a developer proposes using deferred update with no checkpoints in a high-
transaction OLTP system. What is the most serious drawback?

options.label: A
options.text: Log scans become prohibitively expensive after long uptime

options.label: B
options.text: Increased disk I/O due to frequent page copying

questions.hint: Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 28

answer.text: Long-running log scans can make recovery expensive.
answer.explanation: ADB30 warns that without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, a long-running system may scan expensive amounts of log history. Deferred update removes uncommitted persistent effects but does not remove that search problem. Page copying belongs to shadow approaches, while shared locks and serializability are independent concurrency concerns rather than consequences of omitting checkpoints.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: High transaction volume and long uptime can produce costly recovery log scans without a valid boundary.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Frequent copy-on-write pages characterize shadow updating rather than the absence of checkpoints in deferred update.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Omitting checkpoints does not inherently prohibit shared locks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: View serializability is a concurrency-order property, not inherently lost by this checkpoint omission.

evidence.quote: A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.
Without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, long-running systems may need expensive log scans; deferred update does not avoid that problem.
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.

questions.stem: Which listed techniques use transaction logs for recovery under the course model? Interpret Deferred Database Modification as conventional logged deferred update with no-force. Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 46

answer.text: B. ARIES Recovery Algorithm; D. Deferred Database Modification
answer.explanation: ARIES relies on WAL and log-driven analysis, redo and undo. Conventional logged deferred update also uses recorded updates for redo of committed work, with no undo of uncommitted persistent changes. Both therefore belong to the requested category. Shadow paging preserves old page mappings instead, while recovery in multidatabase systems names an environment rather than a particular log-based technique.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multidatabase recovery describes an environment rather than one specific recovery technique.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ARIES explicitly uses WAL and log-driven analysis, redo and undo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves committed page maps rather than being the conventional log-based technique.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deferred modification can use logged changes for redo after commitment.

evidence.quote: Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.
ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table.
It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.

questions.stem: Which type of fragmentation divides a relation into subrelations containing subsets of its columns, repeating a key or row identifier so the original rows can be reconstructed?
questions.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 82

answer.text: D. Vertical
answer.explanation: Vertical fragmentation divides a relation by columns. Repeating a key or row identifier allows corresponding pieces to be joined back into the original rows without spurious matches. Horizontal fragmentation divides rows instead. Replication creates copies, while location transparency hides where data resides. Hiding a column split would be fragmentation transparency, but the question asks for the split operation itself.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replication copies data rather than dividing its columns.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Location transparency hides sites rather than splitting a relation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets with a reconstruction identifier.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Hiding this column split from queries is fragmentation transparency; the split itself is a data-design operation.
Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained.

blocks.text: An object combines identity, state and behavior.
A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance.
The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime.
Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity.
Persistence lets an object survive beyond the program execution that created it.
An OODBMS adds durable storage, transactions, querying and controlled sharing to object concepts.
It does not primarily present objects as rows and tables.
An object-relational DBMS extends a relational system with richer types; ORM maps programming objects into relational tables.
These three approaches differ.
Complex CAD or multimedia structures can suit an object model, but many-to-many relationships alone do not require abandoning relational design.
University of Pittsburgh: Object-oriented databases
Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details.
Account.withdraw(amount) can enforce a balance rule while hiding its storage.
Abstraction presents the relevant contract—what withdrawal does—without exposing how it is implemented.
These ideas overlap in information hiding, but combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation.
An association links objects, often through references; Department.employees can reference Employee objects.
It is different from inheritance, which means an is-a relationship between types.
Methods can invoke operations on other objects, supporting collaboration.
A class defines structure and behavior; an attribute describes state; a method implements an operation.
Do not treat each of these as an interchangeable name for the whole object.
University of Pittsburgh: Object-oriented databases
Inheritance derives a subtype from a superclass, reusing applicable attributes and behavior.
GraduateStudent is a Student; association instead says Student belongs to Department.
EER teaches inherited attributes and relationships, while a programming object model also specifies behavior.
Subtype polymorphism lets a superclass/interface reference denote objects of different compatible subclasses.
The same operation can dispatch to different implementations: Shape.area() calls Circle.area() or Rectangle.area() according to the actual object.
This is not arbitrary conversion of an object into an unrelated class, nor dynamic class mutation.
Inheritance establishes a subtype relationship; polymorphism uses that relationship through a common interface.
Distinguish inheritance as a structural relationship from polymorphism as a use of that relationship at runtime.
Oracle Java Tutorials: Polymorphism
In a common object model, an object is described by (OID,type constructor,state).
An atom is one basic value, such as an integer, real, Boolean or string.
A tuple constructor groups named component values into one structured record, such as (Street:'A',City:'B').
It is not a collection of records.
A set is an unordered collection without duplicates; a bag allows duplicates; a list has order; an array provides indexed positions.
Constructors can be nested to represent complex objects, such as a tuple with a set of phone numbers.
An array is not an atomic constructor merely because stored as one programming variable.
A type constructor defines the shape of a value; it is not the same as an executable constructor operation that creates a new object.
University of Pittsburgh: Object type constructors
Object Definition Language (ODL) is the ODMG schema-definition language for object databases; it describes interfaces/classes, attributes, operations and relationships.
Object Query Language (OQL) expresses queries.
Host-language bindings connect these definitions and operations to languages such as Java or C++.
Defining a logical schema is different from implementing its storage.
An inverse declaration pairs opposite directions of the same relationship.
Conceptually, Department.employees is inverse to Employee.department: when an employee belongs to department D, the corresponding employee appears in D's collection.
The declaration expresses relationship consistency; it is not an inheritance keyword or an ordinary scalar attribute.
An MCQ calling ODL both a DDL and a language for developing logical schemas offers overlapping true descriptions, so its exact wording matters.
Juniata College: Object Databases
A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work.
Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.
A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.
Active means operations are executing.
Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured.
Committed means commitment succeeded.
A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt.
Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation; recovery supports atomicity and durability.
Transaction management is the broader subsystem, so both it and recovery management can be legitimate answers to broad responsibility questions.
Worked example

items.text: A=5,000 and B=8,000 become 4,250 and 8,750 after transferring 750 from A to B. Both balances total 13,000. Unchanged or reverse-transfer balances can also preserve that sum; only the requested debit/credit implements the specified successful transfer.
